Real request and error figures from the observability system

records.title: The operational metrics GET names the lifetime claim count of all organizations request_count (its own header says request_count is a proxy that returns a placeholder), derives error_rate from the number of claim updates whose message contains the text error or failed divided by the number of status changes in 24 hours, and runs its five reads under Promise.allSettled so that a rejected read is replaced by 0 (or an empty queue list) and the response is still 200 with window 24h, so an unreachable database or job queue reads as a healthy zero and the figures are not request counts or error rates.

The operational metrics GET compares the x-service-key header with AI_SERVICE_KEY using ===, which is not a constant-time comparison (lib/api/secret-compare.ts holds secretsEqual for this purpose and the route does not use it), accepts that one shared key as authority over the figures of every organization, and when the data queries throw returns 500 with detail set to String(err), so the text of a database or queue error reaches every caller that passed the check.

The churn-risk routes score a named member with a TensorFlow network that has no trained weights in the repository: loadChurnModel reads model.json from disk and, when it is absent (no code calls saveChurnModel), builds a new network and fits it for 50 epochs on 150 generated examples whose feature values are drawn with Math.random from hand-written ranges (the medium-risk labels are Math.random() > 0.5 ? 1 : 0), the normalisation constants are literals and confidence is Math.abs(churnProbability - 0.5) * 2; the POST stores the result with isPredictionFromML true and returns it as aiGenerated with source ml, so a risk level for a named person is presented as the output of a trained model when it is the output of a randomly initialised network fitted on invented data, and the interventions derived from it (priority outreach, a dedicated steward) attach to that person.

The churn-risk SQL names columns and values that no schema file in the repository defines: the POST reads profiles.organization_id, full_name, union_tenure_years and member_age (profiles is the billing profile and has none of them) and claims.resolution_notes, counts claims with status withdrawn (a value the claim_status enum does not have) and inserts user_id, model_type, model_version, prediction_value, confidence_score, predicted_at, response_time_ms and features_used into ml_predictions, and the GET filters ml_predictions on model_type and predicted_at and joins profiles on user_id, while the declared ml_predictions shape, which the storage authority register calls canonical, has none of those columns, so on a database built from the repository these statements are rejected and the route answers 500 instead of a prediction; the intervention strings the POST stores and returns also carry garbled characters (UTF-8 emoji decoded as Latin-1 text).

The churn-risk routes build a risk profile of a named member from that member case history (claim count, resolution rate, days since the last claim, a satisfaction figure the SQL itself labels simulated and infers from claim status and a resolution-notes text match, and a count of withdrawn claims), store the case-derived features in ml_predictions.features_used and return the member name, risk score, contributing factors such as inactive for N days or N negative feedback incidents, and tenure to any officer, with no record of what members are told, whether they consented, which office may act on a score or how long a score is kept.

The churn-risk invocation audit is a separate write outside the data transaction and ahead of the checks that decide whether the call is valid: auditAIInvocation writes an audit_logs row through auditLog and its own tenant context before the GET checks the organization and before the POST validates the body, so a rejected request leaves an AI invocation record with outcome success, the GET (a read method) writes a row on every call, and the POST prediction row and its persistAtomicAudit record commit in a second, unrelated transaction; the auditRefId returned in the response metadata names the first record, not the committed prediction.

The churn-risk handlers are registered with withRoleAuth at the officer floor but ignore the context it supplies (the parameter is named _context) and resolve the user and organization a second time with getCurrentUser, the GET counts claims per member with a subquery (WHERE member_id = p.user_id) that carries no organization predicate and runs through the shared database client outside any organization context, the limit query parameter is parseInt of the raw string with no number check and no upper bound, and neither handler applies guardAiFeature although the sibling model routes apply one.

The SLA breach risk POST returns computeSlaBreachProbability, a sum of literal weights over four caller-supplied values (priority, hoursRemaining, transitionCount, hasPreviousBreaches; featureRefs is only required to be a list of strings of two characters or more), clamped to 0.01 to 0.99, together with a constant confidence 0.78, bounds of plus and minus 0.08 and a model object with type, version and trainedAt taken from a model_metadata row the route inserts with scoring heuristic_v1 when none exists, so arithmetic over unverified inputs is presented as a model prediction with a confidence and a training date, and a steward can obtain any score (including 0.80 and above, which the realtime alerting sweep counts as an imminent breach signal) by choosing the inputs.

The SLA breach risk POST accepts caseId as any GUID, never reads claims or grievances to check that it exists or belongs to the organization, and does not store it on the ml_predictions row (the table has no case column; the id appears only in the audit record details and the response), so a score is not attached to a case, the GET cannot list the predictions of a case, and the feedback route cannot check that a prediction belongs to the case it is later said to be about.

The SLA breach risk POST and feedback POST take modelVersion from the caller (default sla-risk-v1, any non-empty string), look up model_metadata by organization, type sla_breach_risk and that string, and insert a new model_metadata row when none exists (the POST with the caller featureRefs as parameters, the feedback with empty parameters), so a steward creates unbounded model rows, the version recorded for a prediction is whatever was typed, and feedback can be recorded against a version the prediction was never made with.

The SLA feedback POST lets a steward submit feedback for the same prediction any number of times (nothing records that a prediction already has feedback), takes actualBreach and resolutionHours from the request body with no check against the case, and folds each submission into a running mean absolute error by reading the model_metadata parameters JSON and writing it back without a row lock or version check, so two concurrent submissions overwrite one another observation count and a steward can move the quality score and the retrain recommendation at will.

The SLA feedback routes compute meanAbsoluteError, a qualityScore written to model_metadata.accuracy, retrainRecommended after 30 observations with an error above 0.25, a trainingDataQueue of the last 200 submissions (each with its free-text comment and submitting user id) and a retrainSignal, and the GET returns them as the model feedback summary, but no code reads trainingDataQueue or retrainSignal and the scoring function that produced the predictions is a fixed formula that never reads model parameters, so no retraining can follow from the signal and the accuracy figure describes a formula that stays as it is.

The SLA feedback POST updates model_metadata inside withRLSContext, which when UE_CANONICAL_BOOTSTRAP_V2 is 1 runs the transaction as the union_eyes_runtime role, and the round-58 migration revokes every privilege from that role on model_metadata and grants SELECT and INSERT only (the storage authority register records the same required privileges), so under that configuration the UPDATE is refused with a permission error, the whole transaction including the audit record rolls back and the steward receives a server error for every feedback submission, although the route is the one the register lists as the feedback path.

The SLA feedback POST calls trackPilotEvent after the transaction has committed and awaits it with no error handling: trackPilotEvent inserts into pilot_events through the shared database client imported from @/db outside any organization context (the route holds no tenant transaction at that point, and pilot_events carries a direct organization row-level policy), so when that insert fails the steward receives an error for feedback that was already committed and audited, and a retry records the observation a second time; the pilot_events activity record is therefore written in a separate transaction from the feedback and its atomic audit record, so the audit trail of the submission is split across two commits that can disagree.

The SLA breach risk GET lists the latest 25 stored sla_breach_risk prediction rows of the organization at the member floor with no guardAiFeature feature gate and no enforceAISafety call (the destructured handler argument is only organizationId), where the POST of the same file and both methods of the feedback route apply both, so an organization that has switched the AI feature off still serves its stored predictions to every member.

The ml/query POST forwards the free-text question of a steward (up to 500 characters), an arbitrary context value validated only as z.any(), the organization id and the shared AI_SERVICE_TOKEN bearer to the service at AI_SERVICE_URL, and merges the JSON the service returns (which its own contract says may include the generated sql and result data) into the response unfiltered, with no record of what the service may receive, no data-class or consent decision and no check of what comes back, while nothing in the repository implements the /api/query endpoint to show that it applies the organization id it is sent; the question and context can name members and cases.

The ml/query POST records its audit through logApiAuditEvent, which only writes a logger.info line (the question cut to 100 characters and the confidence), after the external call and not persisted, and it calls enforceAISafety with userRole member and dataClass internal although the route requires steward and answers over claims, steward workload and settlement data; enforceAISafety reads only the user id, organization id, requested entity organization and canMutate, so the declared role and data class are labels and not controls, and a question that is answered leaves no durable audit record.

The ml/monitoring/metrics GET queries ml_predictions for predicted_at, prediction_correct and assignment_accepted and model_metadata for model_name, precision, recall, f1_score, last_evaluated_at, baseline_accuracy and baseline_confidence, none of which the declared tables have, and joins model_metadata to the per-model figures on model_name with no organization predicate (the table is organization-scoped, and the query runs through the shared database client rather than a tenant transaction), so on a database built from the repository the route fails with a column error, and were the columns present the join would mix the model rows of every organization into one organization figures.

The ml/monitoring/metrics GET substitutes literal figures for what was not measured and reports them as model health: precision, recall and f1 are COALESCEd to 0.80, the status CASE returns critical whenever accuracy is NULL and healthy only at 0.85 and above, and the mapping code turns a missing value into 0, a missing status into healthy, a missing trend into stable and a missing last_evaluated_at into the current time, so a model with no measurements is reported with 0.80 quality figures and a fresh timestamp.

The drift, usage, claim-outcome, timeline, workload-forecast and recommendations routes are the same generic crudRoutes configuration over ml_predictions, so each lists every stored prediction row of the organization whatever its type (page of 50, at most 100) and inserts a caller-supplied row, while its name advertises drift monitoring, usage monitoring, an outcome prediction, a timeline forecast, a workload forecast or recommendations, and nothing is computed, filtered by type or monitored behind any of them.

A steward can insert an ml_predictions row of any prediction type, value, bounds, confidence and horizon through the six generic prediction routes (the body is copied into the insert), and the same table is what the SLA breach risk list returns for type sla_breach_risk, what the SLA feedback route accepts a prediction id from, what the realtime alerting sweep counts under withSystemContext (sla_breach_risk rows from the last 60 minutes with predicted_value at or above 0.80, which raises an organization alert) and what the insights generator reads as the latest 20 predictions, so a caller-chosen row is stored with no provenance and is consumed as a model output.

The declared ml_predictions shape (prediction_type, prediction_date, predicted_value, bounds, confidence, horizon, granularity) conflicts with the SQL files that create the table: db/migrations/20260324_add_remaining_missing_tables.sql, db/migrations/20260507_fixup_create_break_glass_activations.sql and db/migrations/manual/067_advanced_analytics_q1_2025.sql each create it with model_name, model_version and target_date NOT NULL and no default, and migrations-platform/0019 only adds the declared columns (and sets NOT NULL on them only when the table is empty), so on a table created from those files the inserts of the SLA breach risk route and of the generic prediction routes, which supply none of the legacy columns, are refused by the database.

The ml/monitoring/alerts routes name columns and a table that the repository does not define and the GET holds SQL that is not valid: it reads ml_predictions.model_type, predicted_at, prediction_correct and confidence_score (the declared table has prediction_type, prediction_date and confidence), joins a table ml_alert_acknowledgments that no schema file or migration creates, ends two SELECT lists with a trailing comma before FROM and orders by alert_timestamp, which no CTE selects, so the GET answers 500 and the POST, which inserts into ml_alert_acknowledgments, fails with a missing relation, on a database built from the repository.

The ml/monitoring/alerts GET emits a P1 finding with the literal text Data drift detected: Case Complexity PSI = 0.28 (threshold: 0.25) for Claim Outcome Prediction whenever the organization has created more than 100 claims in the last 7 days, whatever the data is (no population stability index is computed), and builds every alert id from the model type and TO_CHAR(NOW(), YYYYMMDDHH24MISS), so a drift figure is asserted from claim volume alone and the id of each alert changes every second, so an alert cannot be referred to twice.

The ml/monitoring/alerts POST requires alertId to be z.guid, while every id the GET generates is text such as perf_<model>_<timestamp>, so no listed alert can be acknowledged; the insert is keyed ON CONFLICT (alert_id) alone, so an acknowledgement of one alert id by one organization blocks the same id for every other organization (the update applies only to the organization own row and a conflict is answered 409), and the POST accepts any GUID the caller types, acknowledging an alert that does not exist.

The ml/monitoring/alerts GET joins ml_alert_acknowledgments on alert_id with no organization predicate and runs the whole read through the shared database client rather than a tenant transaction (the POST uses withRLSContext), so an acknowledgement written by another organization for the same alert id would be shown as acknowledged, with the acknowledging user id and time, in this organization list.

The /api/metrics route is a generic crudRoutes configuration over analytics_metrics that lists the organization stored metric rows at the member floor and accepts a steward-supplied row, while lib/observability/metrics.ts documents the Prometheus (prom-client) metrics as available at GET /api/metrics and lib/public-routes.ts names /api/metrics as a role-scoped infrastructure route, so a scraper pointed at the documented path receives JSON rows of business metric records (including their metadata column) rather than metrics in the exposition format.

The /api/movement-insights/trends route is a generic crudRoutes configuration over analytics_metrics (the organization own metric rows, readable at the member floor and insertable by a steward), while the movement insights dashboard page documents anonymized cross-union trends with a minimum of 5 organizations per trend, no individual organization identifiable and a consent status, reads movementTrends and dataAggregationConsent, and admits only the MOVEMENT_INSIGHTS_ROLES office list, so the API path serves none of the consent, minimum-population or office controls its name and its dashboard describe and returns organization rows under a movement-trends name.

The notification list GET wraps its three queries in a try block whose catch logs and returns an empty notifications array, unreadCount 0 and zero totals as a normal 200 (the comment says the in_app_notifications table may lack expected columns), and a non-numeric page parameter becomes NaN, fails the query and takes the same path; the count GET catches every error with an empty catch and returns count 0; so a failed read is shown to the member as no notifications and no unread items, and the dashboard top bar that calls the count route cannot tell the two apart.

The notification create POST lets a steward insert a row for any non-deleted member of the organization with a caller-written title, message, type, action label, action url and data object taken from an unvalidated body (no schema, no length or shape bound, an unparsable expiresAt becomes an Invalid Date that fails at insert and answers 500), and in_app_notifications has no created-by or sender column and the insert sets none, so the recipient sees a steward-authored message in the same inbox and with the same presentation as a system notification; the acting steward appears only in the audit record, whose details hold the recipient and type but not the text, and nothing limits which members or how often.

The notification PATCH reads read from the body without a schema: a value that is truthy but not a boolean (such as the string false) sets readAt to now and stores the text in the boolean column, a value PostgreSQL cannot parse as a boolean fails at the update and answers 500, and setting read to false never clears readAt, so the stored read timestamp can contradict the flag; the audit record stores the raw read value that was sent.

The notification test POST inserts one in-app row for the calling steward with a fixed title and the message that it verifies that the notification setup is working correctly, but it calls no push, e-mail or SMS channel and reads no device or preference, so a success proves only that a database row was written; every call adds another row with no expiry and no de-duplication, and the response is the stored row, not a delivery result.

The push device collection reads at the member floor and restricts a read to the caller own profile, but its POST requires the steward floor, so a member (the only person who holds the phone) is refused with 403 when the retired /api/notifications/device route sends them to /api/mobile/devices to register; for a steward the insert copies every body field into push_devices apart from the forced profileId (enabled, quiet hours, timezone, lastActiveAt, id, createdAt), an unknown platform value fails the push_platform enum and a user without a profiles row fails the foreign key, both as 500.

Devices are kept in two unrelated tables: push_devices (written by the generic device route) and mobile_devices (written by the sync route), each with its own token, preference and active columns, and neither route exports a PATCH or DELETE or has an item route, so a device or token can never be disabled, archived or removed by its owner or an administrator, a device that passes to another account is refused with 409 by the ownership check on every later registration, and the only code that reads either table for delivery (services/fcm-service.ts over push_devices and lib/mobile/mobile-engine.ts over mobile_devices) is imported by no route, worker or script outside its tests.

The mobile sync GET selects every column of mobile_devices and the POST returns the inserted row, and the device collection GET and POST return the whole push_devices row, so each response carries the device push token (a delivery credential for that device) together with the jailbreak flag, compliance issues, last compliance check and metadata columns; the rows are limited to the caller own devices, but nothing projects the token or the security flags out of a response that a browser or script can read.

The /api/mobile/sync route lists and registers mobile devices and synchronizes nothing: it never touches the mobile_sync_queue table that the mobile engine defines, and its POST refuses a body without deviceToken, deviceId and platform, while the only in-repository caller, the Sync now button in SyncStatus, posts just deviceId (or the text unknown) and platform pwa with no deviceToken, so that request is always answered 400 and the control reports an error whatever the device state.

When the same user posts an existing deviceId the sync POST updates deviceToken, appVersion, osVersion and lastActiveAt but not organizationId, so a user who registers the device while acting in a second organization receives the row still bound to the first organization (the GET filters by the current organization and will not list it) while the audit record is written for the second one; a deviceToken already held by a different deviceId, and a platform, name or version longer than its varchar column, are not checked and surface as raw database constraint failures answered 500.

The /api/mobile/push/subscribe and /api/mobile/push/unsubscribe routes are the same crudRoutes configuration over push_notifications, the push campaign table: the browser client posts the PushSubscription (endpoint and keys) to subscribe and { endpoint } to unsubscribe, neither of which names the NOT NULL campaign columns, so a steward request fails at insert and answers 500 and a member request is refused 403 at the steward floor, no subscription or opt-out is ever stored or removed, and the client never inspects the status, so it marks the browser subscribed after subscribe and unsubscribed after unsubscribe although the server did nothing.

The push campaign GET paths return the push_notifications rows of the organization to any member (member read floor, no owner column, and the table has no user column for the low-role guard to apply), including draft and scheduled campaigns with their name, title and body, targeting (target type, target criteria with roles, statuses, tags and custom fields, topics), the uuid array of targeted push_devices rows, delivery counters and the creating user id, so every member can read unpublished union campaigns and how they are aimed.

The push campaign POST copies the whole request body into push_notifications at the steward floor, so a steward can create a row with status sent, sentAt, targetType all and any totalTargeted, totalSent, totalDelivered, totalClicked and totalDismissed values, and the row then reads as a delivered campaign with engagement figures although no route, worker or script that is imported by the application sends a push (services/fcm-service.ts has no importer outside its tests) and no push_deliveries row exists.

The /api/mobile/notifications route is the generic factory over the notifications table (the scheduled deadline-reminder queue: type, priority, related entity, scheduled time and send status), not the in_app_notifications inbox that /api/notifications serves, so a mobile client that lists notifications receives a different dataset with no read flag or read route; a member sees only their own rows but a steward or above reads every user scheduled notification of the organization, with message text and the related grievance, claim or deadline reference.

The scheduled-notification POST copies the body into the notifications table at the steward floor with no check that the target userId is a member of the organization (the sibling /api/notifications POST makes that check), so a steward can store a row addressed to any user id string, set its status to sent and its sentAt, priority and related entity, and that row reads as a delivered notification although the notification-processing cron that would send scheduled rows answers 501 NOT_IMPLEMENTED.

The top-level /api/negotiations route is a second copy of the /api/bargaining/negotiations collection: the crudRoutes configuration over the negotiations table is identical in both files (member read, steward write, organization scoped, no blockedPatchFields), so the same confidential negotiation records are reachable by two paths and a role, confidentiality or field restriction added to one path leaves the other open.

The negotiation POST lets a steward store strikeVotePassed, strikeVoteDate, strikeVoteYesPercent, mandateExpiry, estimatedCost, maximumCost, status and confidentialityLevel from the request body, and the route reads no vote, poll, mandate or costing record to verify them, so a steward-typed strike-vote result or cost ceiling is stored as the negotiation record and is then returned to every member by the member-floor GET.

meeting_rooms rows store requiresApproval, allowedUserRoles, blockedDates, operatingHours, min and max booking duration and advanceBookingDays, and the room routes let stewards set them, but no route reads or writes room_bookings and the only booking code, lib/services/calendar-service.ts, returns true from checkRoomAvailability and builds an in-memory booking with the comment that production would insert into room_bookings, so a room configured to require approval or to exclude a role enforces neither and a booking is never stored.

A PATCH sent to /api/meeting-rooms/[id]/bookings updates the meeting_rooms row whose id is the path value at the steward floor, copying every body field except the primary key and the organization (status, isActive, requiresApproval, allowedUserRoles, blockedDates, contact person, e-mail and phone, imageUrl, metadata, createdAt), and reads or changes no room_bookings row, so a client that patches a booking changes the room itself and a booking id addresses nothing.

The four OCI routes (intake, assessment, results and report) are wrappers over the OCRA alias handlers, which re-export the ICRA handlers, and each wrapper calls a local requireOrgAccess function that returns the literal true for every request and, for the intake and assessment POST, a validateMutationBoundary whose schema checks only that request.method is a string, so the 401 and 400 branches are unreachable and the file reads as an organization access check over a flow that is in fact anonymous and authorized only by the assessment bearer capability; the OCI paths add a third public name for the same handlers, with the same limits, consent gaps and defects, and no behaviour of their own.

The OCRA e-mail results path re-exports the ICRA e-mail results handler, which accepts any syntactically valid address typed by the caller, with no proof that the caller controls it, and sends a branded message from the platform through the e-mail provider that embeds the caller 30-day bearer capability in the link fragment, so any holder of a capability (the start path issues one to anyone) can make the platform mail the capability link to a third party under a second public path name, limited only by the per-process in-memory allowance, and no decision names who may receive an assessment link.

The peer benchmarks route (member floor) takes the organization to benchmark from the organizationId query parameter and the clause suggestions route (officer floor) takes it from the organizationId body field, and both handlers destructure the session organization as an unused underscore variable and never compare it with the requested id, so the library reads whichever organizations row the request names (and, for benchmarks, the member counts of its peers) and the only boundary left is the row-level-security policy on the organizations table, which the route cannot show was applied to the connection it ran on; a request that names another organization returns that organization data wherever the policy does not hide the row.

The federation discovery route (officer floor) passes a province, a sector and a member-count estimate from the body to a query over every active organization of type federation or congress, ordered by member count and limited to 10, with no organization predicate, and returns each match with its id, name, organization type, province and member count, so an officer of any organization is offered a directory of other organizations by design, and the only thing that narrows it is the organizations row-level-security policy that lets a tenant transaction see its own row; no source decides what a prospective affiliate may see of a federation.

The functions behind federation discovery, peer benchmarks and clause suggestions wrap their whole body in a try that logs the error and returns an empty array, and the peer benchmark and clause suggestion lookups throw Organization not found for an id they cannot see before that catch, so a database failure, an unknown or invisible organization id and a genuine absence of matches all reach the route as an empty list and are answered 200 with success true and a total of 0, and the caller cannot tell a refused or failed lookup from an empty result.

The federation matching function accepts a sector and never reads it (the route documents matching on sector and the filters use only organization type, status and province), adds the reason Similar size category whenever both member counts exist whatever their ratio (the score term is the ratio times 20, but the reason is pushed for a ratio of 0.001 as for 0.9), and awards fixed weights of 40, 30, 20 and 10 points, so the matchScore and matchReasons shown to the officer as grounds for choosing a parent federation are literals that do not follow from the data they name.

The clause suggestion scorer awards 40 points to federation-shared clauses and 50 to congress-level templates and lists the source organization name from the sourceOrganization relation, while the shared clause library policy deliberately gives federation and congress sharing levels no visibility beyond owner, shared-with or public and the organizations policy lets a tenant see only its own row, so those weights can apply only to rows the policy shows (owned, shared with the organization or public), every other source name resolves to Unknown, the sector and province bonuses are added to rows that the filters already restricted to the same sector and province, and the relevance reasons shown to the officer describe a federation hierarchy the data access does not provide.

The peer benchmark function obtains the national average through fetchNationalAverage, which returns the literal table from getFallbackAverage (member count 2500, per-capita rate 45, staff 8, budget 1250000, grievance resolution 45 days) when CLC_API_KEY is unset, when the CLC API answers 404 or an unexpected body, and on any thrown error, and the route returns it as nationalAverage with no flag that it is a fallback; the peer average is computed as a sum divided by the count of peers with a positive member count, which is 0 divided by 0 when every peer has none, and nationalAverage falls back to the peer average when null.

The smart defaults route returns recommended features, suggested integrations and suggested API, document and storage limits from literal tables keyed on an unvalidated organizationType query value (any unknown value falls back to the local table) and a member count taken with parseInt (NaN, zero and negative values are treated as the default of 100), and the feature and integration names, for example benchmark-suite, cross-federation-collaboration, inter-union-messaging, provincial-lrb, wage-data and microsoft-365, appear in no other source file of the repository while no code reads the suggested limits, so the response presents hard-coded suggestions as intelligent defaults for capabilities that no route, registry or limiter defines.

The federation discovery, peer benchmarks and clause suggestions routes record their audit trail with eventBus.emit(AppEvents.AUDIT_LOG, ...) after the work is done, an in-memory event bus whose only retained state is a 1000-entry history, and no code anywhere in the application subscribes to system.audit_log, so no audit row is ever written for these reads of other organization data, the emitted event carries no organization id of the actor, and the comment Emit audit event describes a record that does not exist.

The onboarding events route lets any steward or higher write a pilot event and an atomic audit row named onboarding.event.org_created, onboarding.event.user_invited or onboarding.event.role_assigned for a targetUserId and role that are free strings in the body, without creating the organization, sending an invitation or changing any role and without checking that the target user belongs to the organization or that the role exists, so the pilot event table and the audit log hold attestations that a milestone happened which the caller merely asserted.

The onboarding events payload accepts metadata as an unbounded record of unknown values and the handler spreads it after targetUserId and role when it builds the stored pilot event metadata, so a caller can overwrite the targetUserId and role of the event row with different values than the ones the audit row records, and the same unbounded object is written twice (event metadata and audit details) with no size or key limit.

The onboarding transfers path advertises a transfer operation but is a wrapper that calls the onboarding events recorder behind a requireOrgAccess function that returns the literal true and a validateMutationBoundary that checks only that request.method is a string, so a POST to /api/onboarding/transfers records an org_created, user_invited or role_assigned event for the session organization (the event type enum has no transfer value) and the unreachable 401 and 400 branches read as an access check that is not there; the transfers page route only redirects to the pilot onboarding dashboard.

The onboarding root route is the generic CRUD factory over pending_profiles, the pre-signup profile table keyed by e-mail with the Whop membership id and usage credits, which the CRUD governance table lists as DENIED, so every GET and POST answers 403 before any query, while the SelfServeOnboarding component posts the organization name, type, province, plan and terms acceptance to /api/onboarding and navigates to the dashboard only when the response is ok (a refusal is silent), so the onboarding form has no route that can accept it and the path name does not describe the table behind it.

The onboarding root route sets orgScoped true over pending_profiles, which has no organization column, so the factory adds no tenant predicate: a GET at the support_agent floor would list the pre-signup e-mail, Whop membership id, billing cycle and credit balances of every organization and a POST at the steward floor would insert a profile from the request body; the DENIED entry in the CRUD governance table is the only barrier, and the continuity inheritance route is a second path over the same table, so one governance entry guards both.

The onboarding readiness path advertises an onboarding readiness check but is a wrapper that calls the onboarding root handlers, the generic CRUD factory over pending_profiles, behind a requireOrgAccess function that returns the literal true and a validateMutationBoundary that checks only that request.method is a string, so no readiness is computed anywhere, every GET and POST is refused 403 by the DENIED governance entry, and the unreachable 401 and 400 branches read as an access check that is not there.

GET /api/organizations/[id] checks only that a session user id exists, validates only the uuid shape of the path id, and reads the organizations row of that id inside withSystemContext (the union_eyes_system role that the 0108 policy for the organizations table exempts), so any signed-in user receives the whole record of any organization: contact email, phone, website and address, charter number, subscription tier, billing contact id, the settings JSON, enabled features, member counts, creator id and legacy organization id, with no membership, role or mandate check.

DELETE /api/organizations/[id] lets the administrator of an organization set the status of that organization to archived with no further check, although the PATCH on the same route refuses any change of status unless the caller is a system administrator because lifecycle status defines the institution standing: the delete takes no reason or confirmation, does not look at child organizations (the parent_id foreign key restricts deletion, not archiving), does not require a second approver, and the archived status removes the organization from the canonical organization choices (only status active organizations are offered) and from the billing scheduler, so one organization administrator can take the whole organization out of service.

The organization-scoped guard that the item and roster routes call (requireUserForOrganization, through getUserContextForOrganization) finds the caller membership with only the user id and the organization id in the where clause, with no status and no deleted_at condition, so in the legacy (non-canonical) mode a member whose status is suspended or inactive, or whose row is soft-deleted, still passes as a member of the organization with the role the row keeps: they can read the full roster, update or archive the organization when the kept role is admin, and add roster members when it is steward or above; other lookups in organization-utils require status active.

GET /api/organizations/[id]/members requires only that the caller is a member of the path organization (any role, including member, in any status) and returns every roster row with user id, name, email, phone, department, membership number, role, status, primary flag and join dates, with no role floor, no member-directory policy (the organization/members route limits stewards to members of their assigned cases and withholds employment data below officer), no pagination and no read audit; the page and the SMS campaign builder call it.

The item routes under notes/[id], sequences/[id], sequences/[id]/enroll and assignments/[id] take a campaign id as the path id: PATCH at the steward floor rewrites any column of the whole campaign (status, lead organizer, organizing team, outcome figures, archived_at), and DELETE at the admin floor sets the campaign status to archived, so a call to delete a note, a sequence or an enrolment archives the campaign with no reason or confirmation, archived_at is not set, and the archived campaign is still returned by every GET because the read filters no status.

campaign_code on organizing_campaigns is unique across all organizations and is a required column the body must supply, as are campaign_name, target_employer, workplace_location and estimated_unit_size: a code already used by another organization, a repeated code or a body missing a required column makes the insert fail and the route answers an unexplained 500 instead of a conflict or a validation error, and an otherwise complete body that fails because its code is already used by another organization reveals that the code exists outside the caller organization.

The assignments routes assign nobody: an assignment is the lead_organizer_id column (a foreign key to profiles) and the organizing_team uuid array on the campaign row, which POST and PATCH at the steward floor set to any value from the body, with no check that the user is a member or an organizer of the organization, that the organizing_team ids exist, or that the person accepted, and with no assignment history, so any steward can name or remove the lead and team of any campaign in the organization.

The labour board form generator calls /api/organizing/campaigns/<campaignId>, an item path that the repository has no route for (the campaigns route file has no item route), and the organizing console and campaign detail console call /api/v2/organizing/campaigns, which the v2 catch-all answers with a 200 deprecation notice and no campaign data, so those clients load no campaign through the route that exists and show an empty or unpopulated state.

The organizer/impact route is crudRoutes over organizer_tasks: GET returns organizer task rows and POST inserts a task from the body, it reads no case, grievance or satisfaction data, applies no period parameter and returns no current or previous impact object, while the organizer impact page sends period and reads data.current and data.previous, so the page always shows its empty state and no impact figure is computed by any route.

GET /api/organizer/impact returns every organizer_tasks row of the organization to a steward or any role above: the low-role guard holds only callers below steward to their own member_id rows, so a steward reads the assignee, the member id, the related case and grievance ids, the blocked reason and the completion notes of every organizer task in the organization whatever case or grievance mandate the steward holds, and no read is audited.

POST /api/pension/t4a is described as generating a T4A record but generates nothing: it inserts the memberId, memberName, taxYear and pensionIncome exactly as typed (pensionIncome is an unvalidated string, negative or non-numeric values reach the database), may store status generated and a caller-written generated date, derives the income from no contribution, benefit claim or payment, checks neither the member reference nor uniqueness per member and tax year, holds no slip number, box data or document, and transmits nothing to the tax authority, so the member reads an unsupported figure labelled generated as their tax record.

GET /api/pension/trustee-meetings and GET /api/pension/trustee-meetings/[id] require only the member floor and return every column of the meeting rows of the organization, including the agenda, the minutes text and the untyped attendees array, to every member: no role, trustee identity or decision names who may read the minutes of the pension trustees, the list is unbounded, and the trustee administration that would define a reader is not implemented.

PATCH and DELETE on /api/pension/trustee-meetings/[id] let the secretary_treasurer rewrite the minutes, agenda, attendees, date and status of a meeting that is already completed, or delete it permanently, with no state rule, no approval of the minutes, no version of the previous text and no trustee involvement; the audit row lists only the changed field names and the status or the title, so the previous minutes cannot be recovered or compared, and the attendees and minutes are unbounded untyped input.

The pension plan routes accept activeMembers, totalAssets and fundingStatus as typed values (fundingStatus and totalAssets are unvalidated strings written to numeric columns) and derive none of them from the pension_members, contribution or asset records, while GET /api/pension/plans and GET /api/pension/plans/[id] return every plan column, including those figures, the status and the metadata JSON, to any member of the organization, so a member reads plan assets and funding status that are whatever the administrator last typed, with no as-of date or source.

DELETE /api/pension/plans/[id] hard-deletes the pension_plans row for the secretary_treasurer with no check for the enrolments, contributions or claims of the plan (pension_members.plan_id has no foreign key, so the delete succeeds and the enrolments keep a plan id that no longer resolves), no state rule such as terminated, and an audit row that keeps only the plan name, so the funding figures and plan description of the deleted plan cannot be recovered from the audit record.

Creating, changing and deleting a plan, enrolling a member, recording a contribution, issuing a T4A record and keeping trustee meetings are all authorized by one role-title list (PENSION_ADMIN_ROLES is FINANCIAL_MEMBER_DATA_ROLES, the single role secretary_treasurer): no route requires a live financial mandate as the payroll routes do, none calls the kernel authorization, no second person approves, and the pension-authority source states that the trustee-administration authority is not implemented, so the fiduciary acts are one office acting alone on a role string.

The pension write routes store the member and plan references and the money as typed: contributions and T4A rows take memberId as any uuid, with memberName and amount as free strings that are not checked against the organization membership or the enrolment (amount may be negative or non-numeric), enrolment takes planId and userId as any uuid that need not exist or belong to the organization (the table has no foreign key) with yearsOfService, vesting and status typed, and a benefit claim takes memberName, claimType and amount as typed text with no plan, so the rows a member later reads as their own depend on the administrator entering the right identifier.

POST /api/pension/benefits files a claim as pending for any member who holds an organization membership (the claim is tied to no plan, no eligibility check and no amount limit), but no route in the application sets under_review, approved, denied or paid, no notification reaches a trustee or an administrator, and the route says the decision belongs to trustees that are not implemented, so every claim stays pending with no path to a decision and the member receives a filed claim that nothing will process.

None of the pension routes passes a rateLimit option to withApi, although lib/rate-limiter.ts defines PENSION_OPERATIONS for GET and POST /api/pension/* and nothing uses it, so the member own-record reads, the organization-wide administrator reads and the administration writes are limited only by whatever default the platform applies outside the route.

The pension list reads (benefits, contributions, T4A, members, plans, retirement eligibility and trustee meetings) return every matching row of the organization with no limit, offset or page, so an administrator read of a large organization, or the member-floor reads of plans, meetings and eligibility, returns the whole table in one response.

GET /api/pension/members is described as listing the pension members of the organization by plan, but it adds a condition that pension_members.user_id equals the caller organization membership id for every caller including the secretary_treasurer, so the administration console that calls it with a plan id to list that plan members receives only the administrator own enrolment (the member console relies on the same own-enrolment answer to find the member pension id); the description and the administrator use do not match the behaviour.

The member-floor pension reads (members, plans, plan item, retirement eligibility, trustee meetings and the meeting item) query through the shared db import and only the explicit organization predicate scopes them: the row-level-security context is set by withApi only when rlsOrgContext is set or the canonical state context is enabled, so outside that mode the policy that the pension tables carry is not what isolates the tenant and the single where clause is the whole boundary, unlike the own-record reads and the writes that open withRLSContext.

The /api/portal/documents and /api/portal/documents/upload routes are the same crudRoutes configuration over cms_pages (readRole member, writeRole steward, orgScoped true) with no handler of their own: no portal principal or member identity is read, the list is not scoped to documents addressed to the caller, and the two files are byte-identical, so the upload path lists and creates the same page rows as the collection path.

GET on the portal document routes returns cms_pages rows of every status (draft, review, scheduled, published, archived) and every column to any member, including the author user id, the file URL and the content JSON, and never applies the requires_auth and allowed_roles columns of the row, so a document restricted to officers in its own row is listed to every member; pages hold at most 100 rows.

POST /api/portal/documents/upload (and POST /api/portal/documents) copies the request body into a cms_pages insert: no multipart file is read, no file type or size is validated, no malware scan runs, no storage key is derived under the organization, and file_url, content_type and file_size_mb are whatever strings and numbers the steward typed (any URL scheme, any size), so the route reports an upload as created while nothing was received or stored and the row can point members at an arbitrary external or script URL; the file-receiving route /api/documents/upload that validates, scans and stores is not called.

The portal document POST inserts any cms_pages column from the body at the steward floor, including status published, published_at, requires_auth, allowed_roles, view_count and download_count, whereas the content status route moves a row from draft to review only for a content_manager and from review to published only for an administrator under a row lock; a steward therefore creates a published document with no review and no administrator step, and the role that publishes through the workflow is not the role that publishes here.

The commercial transition route lets one platform-tier administrator move a pilot application through contract_sent, contract_signed, invoice_issued and subscription_active, and it inserts a commercial contract (pending_approval, then set to active with signedAt the moment contract_signed is posted, with no signature, acceptance or counterpart step), a platform invoice with status issued for the approved pilot amount and an active organization subscription for the verified organization, while a pilot status of approved, active or completed is written from the state alone; when the billing account, the draft contract or the plan is missing the route only pushes a note that the effect was staged (for example No billing account found; monetization side effects were staged only) and still commits the new commercial state, status, score history and an atomic audit row that names the target state, so the record, the response and the history say the contract was signed or the invoice issued when no contract, invoice or subscription row was written.

The pilot platform tier (applications list, verify-organization, rebind-organization, approve-commercial-terms, commercial-transition and the cross-organization branch of every per-application route) is decided by hasMinRole(system_admin) and by an actor level at or above PILOT_PLATFORM_ACCESS_MIN_LEVEL, which is ROLE_HIERARCHY.system_admin (200), and the hierarchy places platform staff titles such as support_agent (218) and data_analyst (215) above that level, so any account whose resolved role title is one of those titles, or whose user id is in PLATFORM_ADMIN_USER_IDS in the legacy mode, passes every platform check and may read every application with the contact details, bind it to any organization and approve terms; the gate is a role title and no platform-staff mandate or kernel decision backs it.

Before a platform administrator binds an application, the effective owner is responses.organizationId, a value the anonymous applicant typed into the public form (the only reserved key sanitizeResponsesForPublicCreate leaves in place), so an applicant can name any organization id and thereby decide whose stewards pass the same-organization check on the item routes (read, PATCH of non-reserved fields including readinessScore, memberCount and the organization and contact fields, and the artifact, intelligence and reference-profile writes), which lets a submitter place an application and its generated content in the workspace of an organization that never received it.

The public application route buckets its only abuse control, 5 submissions per hour, on the first comma-separated value of the x-forwarded-for header, then x-real-ip, then the literal unknown, and no bot challenge, e-mail proof or captcha is read, so wherever the platform edge does not overwrite that header a caller can send a new value with every request and submit without bound, each submission also creating a HubSpot contact and deal; the limiter fails closed only when Redis is unavailable.

After the insert the public application route awaits upsertContact and createDeal, which send the typed contact name, e-mail address, phone number, organization name, member count and organization type and a deal named for the organization to HubSpot whenever HUBSPOT_API_KEY is set, for any syntactically valid address the submitter typed, with no proof that the submitter controls it, no consent text stored or shown and no decision naming who may receive the contact; the submitter response does not say that the contact is shared.

The public application schema bounds every named field but accepts responses as z.record(z.string(), z.unknown()) and assessment as a passthrough object, with no key count, depth or serialized size limit, and stores responses (minus the reserved keys other than organizationId) in a JSONB column that every later read, proposal, timeline and export returns, so an anonymous submitter can store an arbitrarily large document that the platform-tier list and all per-application reads must serialize.

The proposal, artifact version, package export, reference profile and commercial transition outputs state adoption, activity, champion and risk scores, a renewal and expansion likelihood, an opportunity tier and a qualification, all computed by calculateCommercialSignals and the qualification functions from readinessScore (the applicant self-assessment, typed on the public form or amended by a steward PATCH, and treated as 55 when absent), the stage the administrator reached in the commercial sequence, and memberCount, with championScore and activityScore taken from responses keys that no route writes, so the figures read as measured pilot customer success signals when no pilot activity is an input.

The verify-organization route binds a pilot application to the organization id in the body after bindPilotOrganization checks only that an organizations row with that id exists and that the application is not bound to a different one, and then stamps verifiedBy and verifiedAt; no applicant e-mail domain, contact membership, document or other proof that the applicant belongs to or speaks for the organization is compared or recorded, no reason is required, and the audit row is written under the target organization, so the field named verified states an administrator selection and not a verification.

The approve-commercial-terms route stores the member count as typed by the administrator, an optional subscription plan and a pilot amount that is either the typed number (any value from 0.01 to 9999999999.99) or the lower bound of a price band, as verifiedMemberCount, verifiedPilotAmount and verifiedSubscriptionPlanId on the application with the approver and time, and these values later become the contract value, invoice total and subscription; the only second-person control is that the approver differs from the administrator who bound the organization, no source for the member count or the amount is recorded, and no representative of the applicant organization accepts the terms.

The commercial transition, artifacts, intelligence and reference-profile POST handlers cast request.json() to a TypeScript type with no schema, and persist the caller strings (reason, source, notes, milestone, lessonLearned, objectionRaised, requestedFeature, deploymentBlocker, stakeholder and note) with no length bound into the responses JSONB column and, for the transition, into the audit details; the intelligence handler appends to arrays on every call, so a steward of the claimed organization or a platform-tier actor can grow the column without limit and every later read, proposal and timeline serializes it.

The artifacts, intelligence and reference-profile POST handlers write through withLockedPilotMutation, which locks the application and merges the response keys with a single UPDATE and writes no audit row, and the routes write none, so a steward of the claimed organization or a platform-tier actor can add artifact versions, intelligence notes (lessons, objections, requested features, blockers and stakeholder sentiment) and reference snapshots to a pilot application with no durable record of who did so, although the coverage manifest declares these writes atomically audited.

The reference profile route builds a testimonial, a case study and a benchmark dataset for a pilot application where the testimonial quote is a response key a steward or the applicant can set (referenceTestimonialQuote, authored and role keys are not reserved) or else the literal text that the organization established a repeatable pilot operating cadence with measurable adoption growth, attributed to the application contact name with the role Pilot Sponsor, the time saved is Math.max(6, Math.round(adoptionRate * 0.18)) hours a week (never below 6), and adoption, engagement and health come from a pilot_metrics row or else from the synthetic proposal signals and a 100 minus risk figure; the case study titled as 90-day pilot outcomes and the benchmark record are persisted by POST as a versioned snapshot with a checksum, so quoted words, hours saved and outcomes that no pilot customer said or measured are stored as reference material for the organization with no attestation or consent step.

The champions, friction, metrics and conversion-assessment routes (admin floor) read the organization from the organizationId query parameter and never compare it with the session organization, then call services that run raw SQL over pilot_events through the bare db import filtered only by that id, returning per-user ids with case, update and active-day counts (champions), user ids with the date of the last login or case (friction, full report), unique-user, case and update counts with a daily active user trend (metrics) and the counts that decide a conversion flag (readiness); an administrator of any organization can therefore read the usage telemetry of any organization whose id they know, and the only boundary left is a row-level-security policy that applies only when the request runs under the canonical tenant context.

records.title: The pilot events route lets any member write a pilot_events row of any of 25 event types (including case_created, update_added, first_case_created, org_created, user_invited and role_assigned) with an unbounded metadata object, through a bare-db insert with no audit, and for case_created and update_added only reads metadata.caseId without checking that the case exists or belongs to the organization; the champion detection (3 cases, 5 updates, 5 active days), the conversion readiness flag (3 active users in 14 days, 10 cases, 5 updates, 5 active days), the friction lists and the engagement metrics are computed purely from these rows, so a member can make an organization appear to hold champions and a conversion-ready pilot without creating a case.

The CUPE bootstrap route (system_admin floor, allowed when NZILA_MODE is pilot or demo) resolves the target organization by the slug in a fixture file (cupe-local-123) and, when the body sets reset, deletes every grievance, every organization_members row and every pilot_checklist_items row of that organization with predicates on the organization id alone, with no demo marker, row-origin check, dry run, confirmation or backup, and then re-inserts fixture members (including roles such as admin and president under fixed fixture user ids) and grievances with onConflictDoNothing, so if the organization at that slug holds real grievances or members in a pilot or demo runtime the reset destroys them and the audit row records only the counts the fixture attempted.

records.title: The CUPE bootstrap response reports seeded.worksites as the number of worksites in the fixture although the handler never inserts a worksite, increments membersInserted and casesInserted once per attempted insert even when onConflictDoNothing skipped the row, and returns onboarding checklistInitialized, completed 3 and pending 2 as literals for five checklist ids (org_profile_configured, team_invited, first_case_created, sla_watchdog_enabled and billing_connected) while the onboarding route reads and toggles only seven different ids (org-seeded, users-invited and others), so the seeded rows are never shown by the checklist route, a toggle of a seeded id answers 404, and the same literals and counts are written into the audit details.

The demo-data route (officer floor, pilot or demo runtime) inserts four employers named for real federal departments with e-mail addresses on real government domains (lr-demo@tbs-sct.gc.ca and others) and fictional grievances with named grievants into the employers and grievances tables of the officer organization, the same tables that hold real records, with no demo marker column on either row (only a GRV-DEMO- number prefix and an lr-demo@ address prefix), so the seeded cases are counted as cases managed by the pilot metrics and listed with real grievances, and the purge deletes every row of the organization whose grievance number starts with GRV-DEMO- or whose employer e-mail starts with lr-demo@ whether or not the seed created it.

The pilot current and overview routes report organizerAdoptionRate and memberEngagementRate as the share of organization_members rows whose updated_at falls in the last 30 days (any edit of the row counts as activity), report avgTimeToResolution as the mean of COALESCE(resolved_at, NOW()) minus created_at over grievances created in the last 30 days, so an unresolved case counts as resolved at the moment of the request, count seeded demo grievances in casesManaged, and replace a figure with the stored pilot_enrollments value when no live row exists, with no indication in the response that the figure is a proxy or a stored fallback.

The onboarding checklist PATCH lets any officer mark any of seven steps (contracts-uploaded, employers-imported, integrations-configured, export-verified and others) completed or reopened with a boolean in the body and stamps completedBy and completedAt, and writes a pilot.checklist_completed audit row when all seven are true, without checking that a contract was uploaded, employers were imported, an integration was configured or an export was verified, so the checklist state, isComplete flag and audit trail record asserted steps.

The pilot overview route (officer floor) admits a platform administrator identity or, in the legacy mode, any member of the platform organization (DEFAULT_ORGANIZATION_ID) holding the officer role title, then under withSystemContext lists every actively enrolled organization with its id, name, slug, enrollment date, adoption and engagement rates, cases managed, resolution time, health score and milestones, running three queries for each enrollment and with no pagination, so the cross-organization aggregate is reachable by an officer role title of one organization and no platform-staff mandate or read audit exists.

The pilot current route resolves the session organization with withOrganizationAuth and then runs its enrollment, milestone, member and grievance reads inside withSystemContext, so the row-level policies that scope pilot_enrollments, pilot_milestones, organization_members and grievances to the caller organization do not apply and the explicit eq(organizationId) and the interpolated organization id in the two SQL statements are the only scope.

The pilot feedback POST validates easeRating, category and trigger but passes comment from the body unvalidated and unbounded (any JSON value, no length limit) into pilot_feedback.comment, and the administrator GET returns the ten most recent rows with select() including userId and the raw comment to any administrator of the organization, so free text and the identity of the member who wrote it are returned without a length bound or an anonymity decision.

GET /api/organizations checks only that a session user id exists, applies no role floor and no organization predicate of its own (the only filters are the optional parent and status query parameters), and selects every organizations row visible to the connection inside withRLSContext: in the legacy mode that transaction only sets app.current_org_id and never switches to the union_eyes_runtime role, so whether the list is confined to the caller organization depends on the database role of the connection, and where it is not, any signed-in user receives every organization with its contact email, phone, website, address, charter number, subscription tier, billing contact id, settings JSON, enabled features, member counts, creator id and legacy id, and with include_stats the active grievance count of each listed organization.

records.title: GET /api/organizations returns whatever the tenant context lets the policy show while three administration pages (the new organization page, the edit organization page and the members console) treat the answer as the list of organizations of the union for choosing a parent or an organization: under a connection confined by the 0108 policy the list is the caller own row only, so the parent picker is empty of any other organization and the parent query parameter finds no children, and under an unconfined connection it is every organization (the exposure of DEF-0B10-OPL-01); the route also applies no limit, passes the parent query string to a uuid column unvalidated so that a malformed value raises an unhandled database error and a 500, and lets withRLSContext throw an unhandled error (500) for a user with no selected organization.

POST /api/organizations is limited to a system administrator and commits the organization row and its organization.create audit row in one system transaction, but it reads the body with no schema and no guard on the JSON parse (a malformed body raises an unhandled error and a 500) and writes whatever the body states: name and slug are not checked (a missing name or a duplicate slug surfaces as an unhandled database error), the cached member_count and active_member_count counters, status, settings JSON, enabled features and CLC affiliation are taken from the body, and the parent may be any organization (the parent is only checked to exist, not for its status or its type, and the administrators of the parent have no say in a new child attached to it), so one request can create an organization with invented member counts under any parent of the hierarchy.

POST /api/organizations inserts only name, slug, display_name, type, parent, sectors, email, phone, website, status, CLC affiliation, member counters, settings and features: the description that the new organization page sends is dropped and the sector and jurisdiction that the page sends are stored only inside the settings JSON (the sectors and province_territory columns stay empty), the organization hierarchy admin component sends the type local_union, which the handler refuses with 400, and then tests data.success, a field the handler never returns, so a created organization is not shown and a refused one is not reported; the handler answers 201 with the stored row while the data the caller entered is partly absent from it.

GET /api/organizations/search checks only that a session user id exists and then runs the search inside withSystemContext (the union_eyes_system role that the 0108 policy for the organizations table exempts) with no membership, role or mandate check: any signed-in user can match organizations of every tenant by name or slug (a search with no q returns up to 50 organizations other than the platform type) and receives the id, name, slug, type, parent id, member count, status and sectors of each, so the directory discloses the size, lifecycle status and place in the parent and child hierarchy of organizations the caller has no relationship with.

records.title: GET /api/organizations/search excludes the platform organization type only when no q is given: with a q the filter is an ILIKE on name or slug that returns organizations of every type and every lifecycle status (platform, archived, suspended and inactive organizations included), the q is placed unescaped inside the pattern (a percent sign or underscore matches every row) with no minimum length, the result is limited to 50 with no ordering, no paging and no signal that it was cut, and the statement selects every column of the organizations row (billing contact, settings, contacts) although the mapper returns eight of them.

When the canonical bootstrap flag is not 1, GET /api/organizations/tree checks only that a session user exists and then reads every organization, with no limit and no filter on type or status (platform, archived, suspended and inactive organizations included), through the shared db client with no withRLSContext, no withSystemContext, no membership check and no comparison with the caller organization, and returns the id, name, slug, type, parent id, sector, jurisdiction, description, hierarchy level, member count, status and timestamps of each: the whole parent and child hierarchy of the union is treated as visible to every signed-in user, and whether the result is confined to the caller depends entirely on the row-level-security role of the connection (a confined connection with no organization context returns an empty tree for everyone); only the canonical branch limits the tree to the active private memberships of the caller.

records.title: The legacy branches of GET /api/organizations/tree and POST /api/organizations/switch fill missing values with invented ones: in both a null created_at or updated_at is replaced by the time of the request and a null type becomes union, and the tree also turns a null status into active, a null hierarchy level into 0 and a null member count into 0, so the caller reads a creation date, a type, a lifecycle status and a size that the organization record does not hold.

In the legacy mode POST /api/organizations/switch accepts any organization_members row of the user and the organization as the membership (it reads neither the status nor the removal flag of the row, and does not check that the organization is active), so a suspended, inactive or removed member and a member of an archived organization receive success true together with the organization name, slug, type, parent id, sector, jurisdiction and description, although the organization resolver that later reads the selection cookie requires an active, non-removed membership; an identifier on the PLATFORM_ADMIN_USER_IDS environment list switches to any organization without any membership; and the route stores nothing server side (the client then writes the selection into cookies it controls), so success true reports a validation and not a switch.

POST /api/organizations/switch changes the organization a session works in (the canonical mode revokes the active session and issues a new session row bound to the chosen organization, or writes a provider preference cookie) and neither the route, the canonical selection handler nor rebindSessionOrganization writes an audit record of who selected which organization from which, so the selection of an organization, including a platform administrator selecting an organization they hold no membership of in the legacy mode, leaves no audit trail and the mutation of the session store is not atomic with any audit record.

GET /api/organizations/platform-id returns the constant DEFAULT_ORGANIZATION_ID of the source file as platformOrgId without reading the organizations table: the constant is documented in organization-utils as the Default Organization where all users start (the organization that the non-production fallback assigns to a user with no membership), not as the organization of type platform, so a client that distinguishes viewing the platform from viewing a tenant (the sidebar compares the organization id with this same constant) treats the default tenant organization as the platform, and every signed-in user receives the internal identifier of that organization.

GET /api/platform/metrics/mrr, GET /api/platform/metrics/churn and GET /api/platform/metrics/unit-economics are three copies of one handler that ignores the request, reads no table and returns the fixed object activeUsers 0, requestsToday 0, errorRate 0 under the OpenAPI summary System metrics: a caller that asks for monthly recurring revenue, churn or unit economics receives zeros for three system-usage keys that are none of those figures (no mrr, churn or unit-economics key exists), presented with HTTP 200 as aggregated system metrics, although the subscription event, MRR snapshot and customer acquisition tables exist in the financial service schema and no route under app/api reads them.

The three platform metric routes under /api/platform/metrics are gated at the admin role floor (the organization administrator level of ROLE_HIERARCHY, 140) while the other platform-wide reads (the platform statistics and the platform operator routes) use the platform_lead floor (270): a route of the platform namespace that is wired to the platform revenue tables (mrr_snapshots has no organization column and subscription_events holds the events of every organization) would hand platform-wide revenue and churn aggregates to the administrator of every organization, and the route is a role-title check with no platform-staff mandate.

GET /api/platform/stats admits any caller whose role title is platform_lead or above (a role-title floor, not an issued platform-staff mandate) and returns, for every organization other than the platform type, an organization list with name, type, status, member and active member counts, sectors, CLC affiliation, subscription tier and per-capita rate, together with registered and active user counts, role distribution, grievance, collective agreement and settlement counts, the total monetary value of all settlements and the sector breakdown: the statements run on the shared db client with no organization predicate, no withSystemContext and no withRLSContext (so whether they see every tenant depends on the connection role) and the read is not audited.

The figures of GET /api/platform/stats are named for something other than what is computed: registeredUsers is the count of organization_members rows (one person with several memberships counts several times and removed members are not excluded) and activeUsers is the count of rows whose status is active, totalMonetaryValue is the sum of the integer monetary_amount of every settlement in every status (proposed and rejected settlements included, in no stated currency), and resolved grievances are only those with status settled; the dashboard shows these under labels of users, settlement value and resolved cases, so a count of rows and a sum of unaccepted amounts read as measured facts.

GET /api/portal/dues/balance reads the organization id from the organizationId query value or the x-organization-id header and queries member_dues_ledger through the shared db import with the session user id and that organization id as its only predicates: it does not verify that the caller is a member of the named organization (the sibling pay GET does), opens no withRLSContext, and returns totals and the last five entries, so the answer is bounded only by the user id predicate and by whatever row-level-security the connection role enforces.

The balanceStatus of GET /api/portal/dues/balance is computed as currentBalance <= 0 ? paid_up : currentBalance > 0 ? owing : credit, so the credit branch can never be returned: a member whose balance is negative (overpaid) is reported as paid_up and the credit they hold is not distinguished from a zero balance.

GET /api/portal/dues/pay is described as the member payment history but selects every transaction type of the member dues ledger (charges, credits, adjustments, write-offs and payments) under the key payments, includes the processor payment reference and receipt number, never lists the pending dues_transactions attempts that POST creates, and takes the page size from parseInt of the query value, so a non-numeric limit becomes NaN and the query limit is undefined.

POST /api/portal/dues/pay computes the outstanding balance, inserts a new pending dues_transactions row for the whole balance and creates a Stripe PaymentIntent with an idempotency key derived from that new row id, without looking for an existing pending payment of the member, so every call creates another full-balance intent; the settlement path locks and settles only the paid row and credits member_dues_ledger by that row amount (balance_after is the prior balance minus the amount, with no floor and no comparison with the balance owed), so two confirmed intents credit the ledger twice.
