records.title: POST /api/reports/execute checks each filter against the route allowlist by filter.fieldId while the executor evaluates filter.fieldName when it is present (a registry column of any registry table, qualified or not), so a filter can name columns the route refuses as fields (claims.member_id, claims.assigned_to, organization_members.role, dues_assignments.amount) with the operators in and between that both layers accept, and use the row count and the selected rows as a test of what those columns hold; the route also never reads joins, having, limit, offset or the table qualifier of a selected field, and the executor accepts limit and offset from the caller (default 1000, no maximum), so one request can ask for an unbounded read and the rate limit of 30 per hour is the only bound.

POST /api/reports/execute accepts the filter operators equals, not_equals, contains, greater_than, less_than, between and in, while the executor implements eq, ne, gt, lt, gte, lte, like, ilike, in, not_in, is_null, is_not_null and between and skips any other operator without an error: a filter with equals, not_equals, contains, greater_than or less_than passes the route, is dropped by the executor, and the report is returned with its other conditions and no restriction from that filter, so a report configured for one status, type or period returns every claim or member row of the organization (up to the limit) with success true.

POST /api/reports/execute answers 200 with success false, no data and no row count when the executor fails (an unknown data source of the executor registry, a field or column the table does not have, a join the executor refuses or a database error), because the executor returns the failure as a value and the route copies only success, data, rowCount and executionTime, dropping the error text; the audit event of that run is logged with the event type success and the success flag in its details, an exception is logged as auth_failed with severity high, and a data source the route allowlist accepts but the executor registry does not (members, deadlines, grievances) fails this way for every caller.

POST /api/reports/execute returns the rows of the executed configuration to any caller whose role title is officer or above: the allowlist lets the caller select the email and status of every member of the organization (and claim numbers, types, statuses and dates of every claim), with no per-field authority, no classification or consent check, no row cap smaller than the caller limit and no suppression of small groups, and the only records are a logger line by logApiAuditEvent (user, data source, counts, no rows, no field list) and the generic wrapper record of the path, so what an officer extracted is not durably recorded and no institutional decision names the offices that may reproduce member or claim columns in a report.

GET /api/reports/datasources advertises four sources (claims, organization_members, claim_deadlines, dues_assignments) with fields that the execute route does not match: the route allowlist refuses claim_deadlines and dues_assignments (400) and accepts members, deadlines and grievances that the executor registry does not have, and the registry names columns that the tables do not define (organization_members first_name and last_name where the table has name, claims outcome where the table has resolution_outcome, claim_deadlines current_deadline where the table has due_date and original_deadline), so a report built from the registry as advertised is refused by the route or fails in the database and is answered 200 with success false.

GET /api/reports/datasources is wrapped in withApiAuth only and applies no role floor: any signed-in user with an organization receives the whole registry (table names, column names, types and the joinable tables, including member email, member id and dues amount columns) although running a report needs the officer role, and the organization it checks is the one on the user object, not one resolved for the query; the response contains no rows.

The signature request route reads the signers list from a multipart field with JSON.parse and no schema, and stores each signer name, e-mail address and user id exactly as the sender typed them, with no check that the user id belongs to the organization or to a person whose name or e-mail address matches; recordSignature then binds a signature only by requiring the signer row user id to equal the authenticated caller, so a sender can list their own user id with another person name and e-mail address, record the signature as that person (the audit trail row names the stored signer name and the sender-typed e-mail address as the actor), and when every signer row is signed the document is set to completed with no provider acknowledgment; the same local signing can complete a document that was sent through DocuSign or HelloSign without that provider ever being asked, so a signed or completed record states an identity and an act that no identified counterpart gave.

remaining: Signature bound to the document hash and provider acknowledgement, sealed audit trail, trusted-edge network evidence, signature image source: open

records.title: The signature audit trail rows are plain inserts into signature_audit_trail: the hash_chain column is declared as a future link and AuditTrailService.log never sets it, nothing recomputes the stored file hash after creation or compares it at signing or completion, no row is signed or sealed, and the signer IP address comes from the first value of a client-supplied x-forwarded-for header, the geolocation from the request body and the signature image from any URL the signer posts; the audit route nevertheless returns the rows and, with format=report, a report that the service documents as generated for legal compliance, so a document status, a report and an audit trail are presented as evidence of an e-signature when none of their contents is verified or tamper-evident.

The void path calls provider.voidEnvelope inside a try block whose catch is empty, before and outside the transaction that records the void, and then sets the document to voided and writes the document_voided audit row and the atomic audit row whether or not the provider voided the envelope; a DocuSign or HelloSign envelope that failed to void stays open and signable by its signers at the provider while the organization record, the audit trail and the PATCH response say voided, and the provider status sync then ignores the provider later reporting completed because a voided state is final.

The signature request route has no role floor, no rate limit, no file size or type bound and no approval step: any authenticated user with an organization uploads a file in a multipart form, supplies a title, a description and a list of signers by name and e-mail address, and the service sends the file bytes, the signer names and e-mail addresses, the subject and the message to DocuSign or HelloSign under the organization provider credential, which then e-mails the typed addresses from the organization account, with no consent record for the recipients and no decision naming who may send documents for signature in the union name.

remaining: No approval step and no rate limit; the offices that may send are an institutional decision     (steward floor is an engineering default)

records.title: When no DocuSign or HelloSign credential is configured, or the caller sends provider internal, the provider factory returns InternalSignatureProvider, whose createEnvelope fabricates an envelope id and signing URLs that the service never stores or sends, whose status read always answers sent with no signers, and whose void and reminder methods are empty; the service nevertheless inserts the document as sent, writes the document_sent audit row, and the route answers success true, so signers who are external (no user id) receive nothing and can never sign because recordSignature rejects a signer with no user id.

The request route stores expiresAt, requireAuthentication and sequentialSigning on the document and the signing order on each signer, and recordSignature checks none of them: a signature is accepted after the expiry date, out of the signing order and without the authentication the sender required, and nothing sets the expired status for an internal document, so the options the sender chose and the audit text describe controls that do not operate.

The document status GET calls getDocumentStatus, which for any document that has a provider envelope and is not completed calls the provider and then updates the document status, the signer rows and the audit trail rows (each synchronization commits its own atomic audit under the system-provider-sync actor), so a read by any signer writes rows and makes an outbound provider call on every request, while a provider outage is swallowed and the stored status is returned as current.

The access check and the reads of signature documents, signers and audit rows run through the shared db import with no tenant context and no organization predicate (verifyDocumentAccess, getDocumentStatus, getDocumentAudit and generateAuditReport look the document up by id alone), and access rests on the sender or signer relationship, where a signer user id is whatever the sender typed with no check that it belongs to the sender organization, so a user of another organization named as a signer reads the document status, every signer row and the full audit trail of the organization, and isolation of these reads is not provable from the route or the service.

The document status returns every signer row with e-mail address, IP address, user agent, geolocation, signature image URL and provider identifiers, and the audit route returns every audit row and the report with actor e-mail addresses and IP addresses, to the sender and to every signer, so each signer, including an external counterparty who has a platform account, sees the network address and location of every other signer; the projection removes storage locations and extracted text only.

createSignatureRequest creates the provider envelope, which e-mails the signers, and uploads the file to document storage before the transaction that inserts the document, the signer rows, the audit trail rows and the atomic audit row, with no compensation, so a failure of the insert (for example a signer user id that is not a profile) leaves a live envelope that signers can complete and a stored file with no organization record or audit row, and the atomic audit proves only the local rows.

The document PATCH declares a zod schema (_signaturesDocumentsSchema) that requires a reason and is never applied; the handler reads action and reason from the raw JSON, accepts only the action void, and stores the reason text with no length bound in the document row, the audit trail row and the audit details.

The documents GET returns every document the caller sent and every document the caller must sign, with the complete signer row for the signing side, in one unpaginated response with no limit, so the response grows without bound with the number of requests.

The OAuth callback and the token refresh store the provider access token and refresh token in the text columns access_token and refresh_token of social_accounts exactly as received, with no encryption, no vault reference and no column-level protection (the calendar connection capability has a token-crypto module; nothing in lib/social-media or the social routes uses one), and the Meta, LinkedIn and X authorization requests ask for page management and posting, business_management and rw_organization_admin scopes, so a database read, backup or log exposure yields working publishing and administration credentials for every connected organization account.

The post route at the steward floor validates only shape and length, then publishSocialPost publishes the text, media URLs and link at once to every active account of the organization on each selected platform (the caller cannot choose an account, so every connected page of a platform receives the post), through the platform APIs, with no draft, review or approval state, no check of the content against any classification, no check that a linked document, a media file or a mention names a member who consented, and no record of who in the union decided to speak; the response reports the platform post ids and permalinks as published.

For an X post with media URLs the publisher checks only that the URL scheme is http or https (its comment says it validates the URL to prevent SSRF), then calls fetch(url) from the server with default redirect following, reads the whole body with arrayBuffer with no size, content type, host or address-range check, casts the response content-type header to an image or video type and uploads the bytes to the X media endpoint, so a steward can make the server request loopback, link-local, cloud metadata or private network addresses and any redirect target, and the response of whatever answers as an image or video is posted from the organization X account.

The OAuth callback is a GET that exchanges the code, calls the platform to resolve the identity, and inserts or overwrites the social_accounts row (tokens, status active) with onConflictDoUpdate, so a state-changing request is reachable by a link, and the temporary oauth cookies are cleared before the state, user and organization are compared, so any request to the callback (a forged link or a replay) destroys the pending flow of a connection that is under way; the audit is a logApiAuditEvent call after the row is committed, which writes a log line and no audit row, and the first Facebook Page or LinkedIn organization the account lists is connected without the steward choosing one.

Initiating and completing a connection and listing the connected accounts call logApiAuditEvent with an object holding userId, organizationId, action, dataType, success and metadata cast through any, but that function logs only timestamp, userId, endpoint, method, eventType, severity and details from its argument, none of which these calls supply, so the log line carries the user id and undefined values and the action, organization, platform and record id are discarded; no audit row exists for connecting an organization publishing identity.

Any steward starts the OAuth flow for the organization, and the authorization requests ask for Meta pages_manage_posts, pages_manage_engagement, instagram_content_publish and business_management and LinkedIn w_organization_social and rw_organization_admin, which exceed what posting needs and give the stored token administrative rights over the page; the same floor refreshes and disconnects accounts, and no source names the office that may connect, replace or remove the union public identity.

The disconnect deletes the social_accounts row and its tokens and answers Account disconnected successfully even when the X token revocation throws (the catch is empty), and it never revokes Meta or LinkedIn tokens (the code comments that they need no explicit revocation), so a token that was exposed or that the union intended to cancel stays valid at the platform with no stored copy left to revoke later; the platform post removal for scheduled Facebook posts is not attempted.

The refresh route marks the account expired and writes a token_refresh_failed audit row on any exception, including a transient platform error or a missing refresh token, discards the error and answers a generic 500, and on success sets the account status to active whatever status it held (suspended or rate_limited included); the Meta branch refreshes the stored page token with the user long-lived token exchange.

publishPost inserts the social_posts row after each platform call, so a database failure after a successful platform post is caught as a platform failure and the live post has no row, no audit and a failed result; per-platform failures are caught inside the operation, so the performAuditedOperation outcome record says completed even when every platform failed, and the request answers 500 with the raw platform error text in results when none succeeded but 200 with partial results when some did; the intent and outcome audit is not committed with any data row.

scheduled_for is passed to a platform only for Facebook (scheduled_publish_time); the Instagram, X and LinkedIn branches post immediately, yet the row is inserted with status scheduled, the requested time and no published time, so a post the steward scheduled is live at once while the record says it is waiting, and hashtags and mentions are stored on the row but sent to no platform, link_title and link_description reach only LinkedIn, and campaign_id is dropped.

The post create schema accepts campaign_id and the handler assigns it to an unused variable, the service insert has no campaign column, so no social_posts row ever has a campaign id; the campaign list metrics, the campaign analytics, the post analytics filter by campaign_id and the CSV campaign export therefore count zero posts for every campaign, and the delete guard that refuses to delete a campaign with posts can never fire.

No route, job or service writes social_analytics rows or the engagement counters of social_posts: fetchAnalytics has no caller and every platform branch of it is an empty block with a comment that the transformation is not implemented, the publish insert leaves impressions, reach, likes, comments and shares at their zero defaults, so the analytics read, the post performance read, the campaign metrics and the export answer 200 with empty or zero figures labelled as impressions, reach and engagement, and the summary averages are computed from those zeros.

The campaign analytics read builds platform_metrics and the timeline from post fields named impressions, engagement, likes, comments, shares and engagement_rate, which its select does not return (it selects impressionsCount and the other count fields), so those platform figures are zero or NaN-guarded to zero even when posts carry counts, goal_progress is a constant undefined, and the clicks total is a constant zero.

The campaign create schema accepts goals and status, checks the goals (metric and a positive target), then stores neither: the insert writes no goal columns and sets status to the literal active, requires at least one platform although the schema marks platforms optional, and the response is a success carrying the campaign row, so a steward is told that goals were recorded for a campaign that has none.

The campaign update reads name, description, platforms, dates, hashtags, target audience and status from the raw JSON with no schema, writes any of them (status, a platforms array of any strings, hashtags of any type), calls split on the date values so a non-string answers 500, and a status outside the enum fails in the database as a generic 500.

The analytics DELETE handler writes nothing and exports posts, account analytics or campaigns as CSV or JSON for the date range at the member floor, with no row limit, no rate limit and no audit record; the CSV writer does not neutralise values that start with equals, plus, minus or at, and it looks each cell up by a key derived from the header text, so the campaign export leaves the campaign name, impressions, engagement, likes, comments, shares and clicks columns blank and the account export leaves followers blank, and a zero value is written as blank.

The handler loads the campaign or post by id alone through the shared db import (the post lookup joins the account without an organization predicate) and compares the organization afterwards, answering 403 for another organization row and 404 for a missing one, so isolation of the lookup rests on the later comparison rather than the query and a caller can tell whether a campaign or post id exists in another organization.

limit and offset are parseInt of the raw query string with no number check, no minimum and no maximum, and are passed to the query, so a caller can request an arbitrarily large page, a negative value that the database rejects as a 500, or NaN.

The post delete asks the platform to remove the post and then updates the local row to deleted, so a failure of the local update after a successful platform removal leaves a row that says published for a post that no longer exists, a platform failure leaves the row published and returns only a generic 500, and the intent and outcome audit records are not committed with the row change.

The social media feed route is the generic CRUD factory configured over the communications campaigns table at member floor read and steward floor write, so the feed answers with campaign rows (name, subject, body, segment query, audience count, delivery statistics, status) instead of social posts, readable by any member including drafts and the audience query, while the feed widget expects platform, publishedAt, mediaUrls and hashtags and calls the deprecated v2 path; POST inserts a campaign row, not a social post, and publishes nothing.

Every GET over steward_assignments (the stewards collection and the stewards/[id] item) is configured at readRole member, and the table has no user, member, email or phone column by those names (its contact columns are workPhone, personalPhone, preferredContactMethod and availabilityNotes), so the low-role guard opens the read: any member of the organization, not only a steward or officer, receives the steward assignment rows with the personal phone number, work phone number, preferred contact method, availability notes, free-text notes, the grievance id of a case-based assignment, the appointer, tenure and training dates, and the unit, worksite and shift coverage, with no field projection and no read audit.

remaining: Appointment route owned by the appointing office does not exist; writes answer 405
Officer floor is an engineering default, not an issued mandate

records.title: The stewards and stewards/[id] routes are crudRoutes over steward_assignments: GET returns assignment rows, POST, PATCH and DELETE are refused with 403 because the governance list holds the table read-only, no other route appoints, confirms or ends a steward, and the only code that inserts an assignment row is assignSteward in the steward assignment service (a grievance assignment that sets the type to steward, writes no audit record and bumps a caseload counter on the separate stewards table) which no route calls, so the route names promise a steward directory with appointment and the source offers a read of per-case assignment rows and no way to create the directory.

The stewards collection and item routes configure writeRole steward over steward_assignments and the item route exports PATCH and DELETE with no blocked fields; the only thing that stops a steward from creating, rewriting or archiving any steward assignment (type, appointer, tenure, coverage, notes) is the presence of steward_assignments in the READ_ONLY list of the CRUD governance file, so a role title at the steward floor would become the authority to appoint stewards the moment that list changes.

The survey form tells the member that submitting anonymously means their name will not be visible to their representative, and the submit route stores isAnonymous on the survey row, but no query, service function or route reads the flag: the survey row keeps member_id and the rating and the free text whatever the flag says, the representative performance and ranking routes aggregate anonymous and named responses together, and a representative with one completed survey is returned that one response as an average, so an anonymous response is not anonymous to a steward who knows which claim the representative handled.

GET /api/satisfaction/lro/<lroId> returns the six rating averages, the overall average and the recommend rate of any representative id the steward types in, and GET /api/satisfaction/rankings returns and ranks every representative of the organization who has a completed survey, at the steward floor, with no minimum number of responses, no check that the id is a representative of the organization or the caller, no control over which steward may read the performance of which representative, and no read audit.

getLroPerformance turns a null average into zero (n = parseFloat(v ?? 0)) and computes the overall average as the mean of six values that may all be zero, so GET /api/satisfaction/lro/<lroId> for an id that is not a representative, or that has no completed survey in the organization, answers 200 with totalSurveys 0, six averages of 0, an overall average of 0 and a recommend rate of 0, which reads as a representative rated 0 out of 5 and not as no data.

POST /api/satisfaction (described in its header as an administrator action and in its OpenAPI text as creating a survey for a closed claim) is configured at the steward floor and selects only memberId and assignedTo from the claim: it never reads the claim status, so a survey can be created for an open claim, and when the claim has no assignedTo the lroId in the body is accepted as any string with no check that it names a representative of the organization, so a survey can be created that asks the member to rate a person who did not handle the claim.

GET /api/satisfaction passes only the session user id to getPendingSurveys, which filters satisfaction_surveys on member_id and status pending with no organization predicate and returns the whole rows, so a person who is a member of two organizations receives the pending surveys of both (claim id, representative id, sent time) whichever organization the session is acting in.

The SCIM 2.0 users route authenticates only a browser session at the administrator floor (withApi auth required, minRole admin) and reads neither scim_configurations (bearer token, token hash, expiry, enabled flag, deprovision action, attribute mapping) nor scim_events_log, so an identity provider that presents the long-lived bearer token the schema describes cannot call it, no token is issued, checked, expired or rotated by any route, no SCIM provisioning event is logged, and the route offers only list and create with no get, replace, patch or delete of a user, no groups and no service provider configuration, so a deprovision cannot be sent at all.

GET /api/scim/v2/<organizationId>/Users selects every organization_members row of the organization with no deleted_at and no status condition, slices the page in memory after loading the whole roster, and maps active to member.status equal to active alone, so a member who was removed (deleted_at set) while the status column still reads active is listed and reported as an active user with name and e-mail address, a count that is not a number (count=abc) makes the slice end NaN and the page empty, and a count of zero or less is accepted.

POST /api/scim/v2/<organizationId>/Users inserts an organization_members row whose user_id is the userName string from the body (the membership key that getUserRoleInOrganization matches against the session user id), with the e-mail taken from the body, the role fixed to member and the status active immediately: the identity provider subject is never read, the person does not accept, the userName may be any string including the identifier of an existing user of another organization (who is then made an active member of this one), and a provisioned person whose session user id differs from the userName string can never match the row, while a removed member with the same user id answers 409 as an existing user.

The SCIM create route reads the body with an unguarded request.json() and a type cast instead of a schema: malformed JSON or an emails value that is not an array raises a plain error that withApi answers as a 500, a userName that is not a string passes the presence check and reaches the insert, and no length or format bound is applied to userName, name or e-mail.

PUT /api/settings/organization merges whatever object the administrator sends as body.settings, with no key allow-list and no value validation, into the organizations.settings JSON that other code reads as authority: services/clc/per-capita-calculator reads settings.perCapitaRate (an organization with a rate of 0 or less is skipped) and settings.remittanceDay to compute the per-capita amount an organization with a parent owes that parent, lib/services/entitlements reads settings.credits and settings.nextCreditRenewal as the credit balance that checkEntitlement tests before a credit-requiring AI feature, and the twilioPhoneNumber key attributes inbound text messages, so an organization administrator can set their own remittance rate and day, credit balance and renewal date directly, and the audit row lists only the names of the fields written (settings, name, shortName, provinceTerritory), never a value.

remaining: Native run of the PUT under the runtime role

records.title: The platform settings page saves sessionTimeout, mfaEnforcement, passwordMinLength, requireMixedCase, requireSymbol, rateLimitPerMin and webhookUrl into the organization settings JSON through this route, which answers {updated:true}, and the settings page reads them back with defaults (mfaEnforcement admins_only, passwordMinLength 12), but no authentication, session, password, rate-limit or notification code found in the application reads those keys, so an administrator who sets multi-factor enforcement or a password policy is told the setting is saved while nothing enforces it.

PUT /api/settings/organization takes the body without a schema, accepts an empty string or an unbounded string as name, shortName and provinceTerritory, reads the current settings JSON with the shared database handle outside the transaction that writes the merge (so two concurrent saves overwrite each other keys), answers a missing body or organization as a plain error that withApi turns into a 500, and GET answers 200 with organization null for an organization row that does not exist.

handleInboundSms attributes an inbound text message to the organization whose settings JSON holds the called number under twilioPhoneNumber, selecting with limit 1 and no ordering or uniqueness, and the organization settings route lets any organization administrator write that key, so an administrator who stores the number of another organization makes the lookup ambiguous and the inbound message body and sender number can be stored in the conversation table of the wrong organization.

The security events route is configured for readRole and writeRole security_manager with a header comment that describes a privileged reader and a closed forgery path, but security_events is in the DENIED list of the CRUD governance file, so assertCrudRead and assertCrudWrite answer 403 to every caller including a security manager; the privileged reader of the table is the security dashboard page, which checks hasMinRole security_manager and reads the table with SQL under a system context, so the API the comment describes does not exist and the integrity rule for who may author a security event is held only by the governance list.

The storage/usage and storage/cleanup routes are crudRoutes over cms_media_library: GET returns the media library rows of the organization (file name, file url, type, size, folder, tags, uploader) at the member floor, and neither route sums file sizes, reads a quota, compares a file with the references to it or deletes anything, so a caller expecting storage usage receives a page of rows and a caller expecting a cleanup triggers none; the cms_media_library table is read and written by no code other than these two routes and the upload route.

POST /api/storage/usage and POST /api/storage/cleanup insert a cms_media_library row from the whole request body at the steward floor: no file is received or checked, so file_url (any string, including an external address), file_size, mime_type, uploaded_by (any profile user id) and folder are whatever the caller writes, and a library entry can point at a file that does not exist, at an address outside the application storage, or be attributed to another person.

The support/metrics and support/sla routes are crudRoutes over in_app_notifications: GET returns notification rows (user id, title, message, type, action label and url, data, read flag) and POST inserts one, and no route reads or computes a ticket count, response time, resolution time or service-level figure, so a caller expecting support metrics or SLA compliance receives unrelated notification rows; the figures themselves are computed by getTicketMetrics and getSLAMetrics in the support service over support_tickets, and no route calls that service.

GET /api/support/metrics and GET /api/support/sla hold a caller below steward to their own in_app_notifications rows, but any steward or higher role reads the notifications of every user of the organization (title, message, action url and the data object), unbounded by any relationship to the recipient and without a read audit, so notifications that name a member, a case or a grievance are readable beyond the member they were addressed to.

POST /api/support/metrics copies the body into an in_app_notifications row at the steward floor with no check that the user id is a member of the organization (the sibling POST /api/notifications makes that check), with a caller-written title, message and action url and no sender stored, so a steward can store a notification with an arbitrary link for any user id string and it appears to the recipient as a message of the application.

The four support/tickets route files (the collection, tickets/[id], tickets/[id]/assign and tickets/[id]/comments) are crudRoutes over in_app_notifications: GET lists notification rows (user id, title, message, type, action label and url, data, read flag), POST inserts one, and GET, PATCH and DELETE of tickets/[id] read, rewrite and hard delete a notification, while tickets/[id]/assign and tickets/[id]/comments are configured identically to tickets/[id] so the path suffix changes nothing: assigning a ticket or posting a comment is a PATCH of the notification row with that id, and no route creates a ticket, assigns an agent, records a comment or a history entry, although supportTickets, ticketComments and ticketHistory tables and createTicket, assignTicket and addComment in the support service exist and no route calls that service.

The item routes under support/tickets configure writeRole steward and export PATCH and DELETE over in_app_notifications with the factory organization predicate and no owner condition for a caller at the steward floor, so a steward rewrites the title, message, action url, data, read flag and user id of any notification of any user of the organization (the body is applied through the blocked-field filter only) and an administrator permanently removes it, with no relation between the caller and the recipient and no record of the previous value.

POST /api/upload is the generic crudRoutes POST over cms_media_library at the steward write floor: it reads a JSON body into a media library row (file name, file url, size, mime type, folder) and receives and stores no file, while the public job application page posts a multipart form (the file and the folder resumes) to the path and reads the url of the response as the resume address; the route requires a signed-in steward, answers a JSON object whose row is under data (never a url), and GET on the same path lists the media library rows at the member floor, so an applicant sends a file and nothing is stored or addressed.

The four tax route files (tax/slips, tax/t106, tax/rl-1/generate and tax/cope/receipts) are crudRoutes over per_capita_remittances configured at readRole member, and the table has no user, member, e-mail or phone column by the names the low-role guard looks for, so any member of the organization, not only an officer, receives the whole per-capita remittance ledger of the organization (remittance month and year, member counts, per-capita rate, total amount, GL and CLC account codes, approver and rejecter user ids, rejection reason, payment method and reference, remittance and receipt file urls and notes), 50 rows per page by default and 100 at most, whatever tax document the path names, with no field projection and no read audit; the query parameters the COPE receipt viewer sends (memberId, taxYear) are not read.

remaining: Arrears and health-and-welfare collections now answer 403; their capabilities are not implemented

records.title: The tax/slips, tax/t106, tax/rl-1/generate and tax/cope/receipts routes are the same crudRoutes configuration over per_capita_remittances and differ only in their path: GET returns remittance rows, and POST is refused with 403 because per_capita_remittances is READ_ONLY in the CRUD governance table, so no route issues, computes or stores a tax slip, a Quebec RL-1, a T106 return or a political contribution receipt although the path names promise each, and the one client that calls a path (the tax dashboard opens the COPE receipt path for a member and a tax year) receives a page of remittance rows in which neither parameter is read.

PATCH and DELETE /api/testimonials/<id> are crudRoutes over the testimonials table with orgScoped false and writeRole admin: the table has no organization column, the role floor is resolved inside the caller own organization, and the update and the hard delete are conditioned on the primary key alone, so an administrator of any organization rewrites (quote, author, role, organization, photo, featured flag, visibility, approval time) or permanently deletes any testimonial the platform shows on its public proof page, and the audit row commits under the organization of that administrator; the storage authority reference already records that any tenant own org-admin can edit or delete this platform-wide content and leaves it for follow-up.

remaining: Native run
Real behaviour of the content_manager role in a deployed identity provider

records.title: GET /api/testimonials/<id> selects the row by primary key at the member read floor and returns every column, whatever the row visibility (the column defaults to public and holds other values) and whatever its approval time (null until approved), so any signed-in member of any organization reads a testimonial that has not been approved or is not public, with its quote, author, role, organization and photo; the public proof page does not read this route and describes its content as anonymized composites.

The testimonial approval component sends PATCH /api/testimonials/<id> with status, reviewedAt and reviewedBy (approved or rejected) and reports success, and the testimonials table has no status, reviewedAt or reviewedBy column and carries approvedAt, which the component never sends, so an approval or a rejection records no decision in any column the table has and the route answers success for it.

GET /api/units and GET /api/units/<id> are crudRoutes over bargaining_units at the member read floor and the table has none of the user, member, e-mail or phone column names the low-role guard looks for, so any member of the organization receives every register row with its certification number, body and dates, contract expiry and next bargaining date, chief steward and bargaining chair user ids, classifications, free-text notes and custom fields object, with no field projection and no read audit.

POST /api/units and PATCH /api/units/<id> are configured at writeRole steward with the whole body copied into the row, so any steward of the organization creates a bargaining unit or rewrites its certification number, certification body and dates, current collective agreement id, contract and bargaining dates, member count, chief steward and bargaining chair, and an administrator archives it, with no check that the caller represents the unit and with the audit row listing field names and no values.

GET /api/worksites and GET /api/worksites/<id> are crudRoutes over worksites at the member read floor, so any member of the organization receives every worksite row with the site manager name, e-mail address and telephone number, the address and coordinates, the employee and shift counts, free-text notes and the custom fields object, with no field projection and no read audit, and the worksite management screen and the unit and committee screens load the whole list from the route.

POST and PATCH on the unit and worksite routes copy the body into the row, and employer_id, worksite_id, chief_steward_id and bargaining_chair_id are foreign keys to the employers, worksites and profiles tables that carry no organization condition, so the row can name an employer, a worksite or a person of another organization (the foreign key check passes for any existing id) and the register then joins organizations that have nothing to do with each other.

The wcb/claims and wcb/claims/[id] routes are crudRoutes over wcb_claims configured at the steward floor for reads and writes (the collection declares an owner column workerId, the item route none), and wcb_claims is DENIED in the CRUD governance table, so assertCrudRead and assertCrudWrite refuse every call with 403 before a query or an audit row, for stewards and administrators alike; the route header describes a claim collection a steward lists and creates, the claim holds the medical and prognosis detail of an injured worker, and if the governance entry is ever lifted every steward of the organization would read and rewrite every claim (the item route has no owner condition), with no relation to the representative who holds the member case.

GET /api/wcb/assessments and GET /api/wcb/assessments/<id> are crudRoutes over wcb_employer_assessments at the steward read floor, so any steward of the organization (not only the officers who record the assessments) receives every assessment row with the premium rate, assessable payroll, premium due, experience rating, surcharge or refund, due and paid dates, status, document ids and the metadata object, with no field projection and no read audit.

GET /api/targets/summary is configured at the member floor and returns every kpi_configurations row of the organization with the whole row spread into the response (`...cfg`): the calculation record (formula, aggregation and filters), the alert recipients (user ids or e-mail addresses), the id of the creator and the dashboard layout reach any member of the organization, not the officers who create targets, with no field projection and no read audit.

The summary takes the current value of a target from the latest analytics_metrics row of the organization whose metric_type text equals the target metric type (one query per target through the shared database handle) and applies neither the data source (claims, members, financial, custom_query) nor the calculation the target declares, so a target is judged against whatever row carries the same type name, and a row of another unit or period that shares the text is read as the current value; the progress figure divides that value by the target value.

computeHealth returns critical when the current value is at or below the critical threshold, at risk when it is at or below the warning threshold and on track otherwise, for every target: a target whose good direction is downward (resolution time, backlog, grievance count) is reported critical when its figure is low and on track when its figure is high, and the route stores no direction.

POST /api/targets stores a free-form calculation record (any key and value, defaulted to a sum), an alertEnabled flag and a data source, and the summary route reads none of the calculation or the data source and no code found reads alertEnabled to send an alert: the insert writes no alertRecipients value at all, so a target created with alertEnabled true promises an alert that no recipient list and no sender exists to deliver.

PATCH /api/targets/<id> compares the path id with the uuid column kpi_configurations.id without a shape check, so a malformed id raises a database error that the wrapper answers as a 500 instead of a 404, and the route offers no way to edit, rename or delete a target: the only change available after creation is the active flag.

GET /api/users/me/organizations, in its legacy branch (entered whenever UE_CANONICAL_BOOTSTRAP_V2 is not 1), links membership rows to the caller when the caller has none: it takes the e-mail address from the identity provider user (or the profile row), selects every organization_members row of any organization whose lower-cased e-mail equals it and runs an update that sets user_id to the caller on all of them, with no condition on the current user_id (a row already bound to another person is rewritten), no verified-address check, no role limit, no organization limit and no audit record; if no row carries the e-mail, a second statement sets user_id to the caller on every membership of the legacy user id of any profile that shares the e-mail; the response then lists the organizations and the roles that were taken, and the whole sequence runs inside a GET with the shared database handle.

remaining: The test that asserted the self-healing was replaced by tests that assert it never happens

records.title: In the legacy branch a user id listed in PLATFORM_ADMIN_USER_IDS receives up to 500 organization records (name, slug, type, parent, sector, jurisdiction, description) whatever their memberships, and every other caller causes the route to select the whole organizations table and filter it in memory by the ids and slugs of the caller memberships, so the cost grows with every organization of the platform and the platform list is held by an environment list the application cannot audit.

The legacy branch logs the full e-mail address of the caller (email: userEmail) when it links memberships by e-mail and a three-letter preview of it in another line, together with the user id, so a log reader receives the address that the re-binding was made on.

The response replaces a missing createdAt or updatedAt of an organization, and a missing joinedAt and createdAt of a membership, with the time of the call (new Date().toISOString()), so a record without a stored time is returned with a time that never existed.

The /api/v2/[...path] catch-all is exported as GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE by one handler that answers HTTP 200 with a deprecation object for every method and path: the dues report page posts /api/v2/admin/reports/generate and treats a response that is ok as a generated report, the user role selector puts a role change to /api/v2/admin/users/role and shows the toast Role updated on an ok response, and the staff page posts remittance approve and reject to /api/v2/clc/remittances/<id>/approve and /reject and logs Approved remittance on an ok response, while the file that builds a 410 Gone response (goneResponse) exists and the catch-all never calls it, so a write to a removed path is reported to its caller as a success and nothing is written.

remaining: Frontend callers of removed /api/v2 endpoints now fail visibly; see functionalGaps

records.title: GET on a removed /api/v2 path answers HTTP 200 with an object whose keys are _deprecated, _message, _sunset and _canonical, where the callers (the push device manager, the social media post composer, the benchmark and scheduled report consoles, the federation remittances and compliance pages) read the body as the list or figures they requested, so a console renders an empty state or no data with no signal that its endpoint was removed.

The catch-all calls logDeprecatedAccess(v2Path, request.method, canonical) with no user id and no organization id and does not await it, and logDeprecatedAccess swallows a failure of the audit write, so the api.deprecated_access event names a path and a method and no actor, and its loss is silent.

The deprecation module holds the sunset date as a constant (2026-07-07) that it prints in the body and the Sunset header, and nothing compares it with the current time or changes the answer after it, so the route keeps answering 200 with a sunset that has passed and no removal is scheduled in source.

GET /api/tenant/current answers HTTP 200 with an org whose name, slug and subscriptionTier are constant null and whose features list is empty, and an availableOrgs list that holds only that same org, so a legacy client that reads the organization name or tier receives a success with no data; the route reads no organization row, and no caller in the application calls it.

GET /api/test-auth is a plain route (no wrapper, no role floor, no production guard) that any signed-in user can call: it sends the session token as a bearer to the Django address held in the NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL build variable (localhost:8000 when unset), returns the status and body of the backend health and /me/ answers, the session user id and organization, whether a token exists and the text of any fetch error (String(e)), so the response discloses backend addresses and error details and the diagnostic ships in every build.

GET /api/union-eyes/queue-status accepts either the service key header or any signed-in session (requireApiAuth with no role, no organization requirement), and returns the pending, active, failed and retry counts of the whole background queue, the per-queue counts and the task id, task name, status and completion time of the 20 most recent failed tasks, which are platform-wide operational data not scoped to an organization, to a signed-in member.

The queue status route sends every error, including the refusal that requireApiAuth throws for a caller with no session, through one catch that answers HTTP 503 with availability error and detail String(err), so an unauthenticated call is reported as an outage and the text of the underlying error (a connection string error of the queue backend, for example) is returned to the caller; when no Django address is configured the route answers 200 with availability not_configured and a null queue.

The service credential of the route is the AI_SERVICE_KEY environment value, the same key that the AI service uses, compared with the request header by a plain equality (===) and not a constant-time comparison, and the control plane sends it on every telemetry call, so one key opens the queue figures and the AI service and cannot be rotated for one without the other.

POST /api/triage-designations passes caseAssigneeEligible (the case policy role that may add an internal note, or ue_case_assignee_authorized in the canonical branch) as the eligibility test for a designation of either scope, while the message queue decides use of a messages designation with the conversation assignee roles (membershipStillEligible), so a messages designation can be refused to a person who is an eligible conversation assignee and granted to a person who is a case assignee and not a conversation assignee, whose designation then grants nothing.

grantDesignation closes a lapsed live designation by setting revokedAt to now and revokedBy to the string system:expiry before the new grant, in the same transaction, and writes no audit row for the closure (only the grant is audited), so the end of an expired designation is a data change with no audit record and a revoker value that is not a user.

DELETE /api/triage-designations takes the designation id from a JSON request body (body: revokeSchema), a pattern that HTTP intermediaries and many clients drop or ignore for DELETE, and the route has no path id; no caller in the application sends the request.

The vocabulary routes serve, as reference data of the grievance system, hard-coded service-level hours (24 hours for critical, 48 high, 72 medium, 168 low), severity legal-review flags, per-role canAssign, canEscalate and canSettle flags for roles named member, steward, chief_steward, business_agent, officer and admin, and a status machine with the roles allowed to make each transition, from a package whose header calls them defaults, with no cited source, no approval and no relation to the roles the application enforces; the flags are not read by any enforcing code found, and a client that treats them as the institution service levels or permissions would present an unsourced figure as institutional.

Every vocabulary route sets Cache-Control public with max-age 3600 on a response that is behind a signed-in session, so a shared cache or proxy may store and serve the response to callers without a session for an hour.

getCUPEVocabulary sets lastUpdated to the time of the call and version to the constant 0.1.0, so the full vocabulary route reports a last update of now on every request and a version that does not change when the content changes.

POST /api/voice/transcribe, at the steward floor, applies no rate limit and no entitlement check and writes no audit record, while the sibling upload route applies a rate limit and an entitlement check: a steward (or a script holding a steward session) can send repeated 25 MB recordings, each up to the 60-second function limit, to the speech service with no count and no record of who transcribed what.

The transcribe response sets duration to audioFile.size (the size of the upload in bytes, with the comment Approximate), so a caller that reads duration receives a number of bytes presented as a length of time.

Both voice routes read the uploaded recording into memory and send it to an external Azure service (the speech service in the transcribe route, an Azure OpenAI Whisper deployment in the upload route), and the recordings are spoken claim descriptions that can name a person, an employer and a medical or disciplinary matter: neither route records a consent, names a processor agreement or region, records the disclosure or states a retention, and the upload route logs the body of a failed processor answer.

POST /api/voice/upload checks the ai_search entitlement of the organization (and labels a refusal voice_upload) for a transcription feature, and checkEntitlement only reads settings.credits and consumes none, so the check neither meters the transcription nor reflects a voice entitlement; no caller of the route exists in the application.

POST /api/workspace/telemetry accepts the allow-listed event name and logs every allow-listed payload key, of which tab and timestamp are written as the client string with no length bound or format check (route is checked against the static route list), with no rate limit, so a member can write arbitrarily long strings of their choice into the application log at any rate, and the figures the route exists to produce live only in log lines.

For a workbook with no claimed_by_user_id, resolveClaimedWorkbookAuthority returns the preclaim authority from the workbook identifier alone, so GET, POST, PATCH and DELETE on /api/workbook/<id>/memory-holders run in the system context for any caller who presents that identifier, with no session, with no guardPublicIntake or other rate limit (the route files import none), and auditClaimedWorkbookWrite returns at once for a preclaim authority so the create, update and delete are not recorded; the same identifier is returned by the public start route and placed in the checkout redirect addresses, and each write may carry a display name and notes of up to 4,000 characters.

After the claim, a same-organization peer is any signed-in person for whom getOrganizationIdForUser returns the claimed organization (that function selects an organization by a client cookie after a membership check): resolveClaimedWorkbookAuthority applies no role floor, and the memory-holder routes then let that person list, create, change and delete holders in the system context, with a display name and notes naming individuals who have no notice that they are recorded, and the PATCH and DELETE audit rows are written only when a row changed.

POST /api/workbook/start accepts consent as an optional object (consentToPersist and a time), inserts the workbook whether or not the object is present or true (consent is stored as null when absent) and logs only the workbook id and locale; no route of the workbook product reads workbooks.consent before it stores a memory holder, creates a checkout session or exports, so the consent the visitor gave or withheld changes nothing the product does.

guardPublicIntake keys its per-client limit (20 starts per hour, 10 checkouts per hour) on the first of cf-connecting-ip, x-real-ip or the first x-forwarded-for entry, all request headers a client can set when the application is not behind a proxy that overwrites them, and neither public route reads a challenge token, so a caller can create workbooks and open Stripe checkout sessions at a rate the limit does not bound.

POST /api/workbook/checkout reads the workbook through the shared database handle (import { db } from '@/db') outside withSystemContext, withRLSContext and withClaimedWorkbookAccess, so the handle is the pooled runtime connection with no app.current_user_id; the closure migration creates the user isolation policy on workbooks over claimed_by_user_id, whose select policy compares that column with app.current_user_id, so an unclaimed workbook (the only kind a buyer has before paying) is not visible to the read and the route would answer 404 for it; the start and claim routes use withSystemContext for the same table, and the runtime proof of the policy is outstanding.

POST /api/workbook/checkout sends the workbook identifier, which is the bearer credential for the memory holders of an unclaimed workbook, to Stripe in metadata.workbook_id and in the success and cancel addresses (/workbook/<id>?tier_unlocked=workbook_self_guided), so the credential is held by the payment processor, appears in the browser history and referrer chain of the buyer and is logged with the session id, and no source states the processor agreement or the lifecycle of the identifier.

When NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL is not set the checkout success and cancel addresses fall back to http://localhost:3000, and the route tests only that the workbook is not already at the self-guided tier, so each call creates a new Stripe session with no pending-session or idempotency check and a buyer or script can open any number of sessions for one workbook.

POST /api/workbook/<id>/claim requires a session but applies no rate limit and reads the body with request.json() without a size cap, and a request whose id and token match a row but whose claim has lapsed is answered 409 or 410 while a miss is answered 404, so a signed-in caller can try claim tokens against an identifier at the speed of the application.

GET /api/workbook/<id>/export builds a PDF of the carrier register (role, criticality, tenure, successor and the free-text responsibility of every memory holder, with the cartography) for a claimant or any same-organization peer and writes no audit record of the read; loadWorkbookModules also selects the display name of every holder into memory although the template does not print it.

The start, checkout and claim routes write the workbook identifier, which is the bearer credential of an unclaimed workbook, to the application log (with the locale, the Stripe session id, or the user id and organization id), so anyone who reads the log can use the identifier on the memory-holder routes until the workbook is claimed.

ue_authority_reviews holds the complainant, the adverse parties and the privileged classification of every review of an organization, and the only row-level-security policy on it is the organization-only policy ue_create_direct_org_rls_policy (migration 0020) while the storage-authority manifest requires SELECT on the table for the tenant runtime role; the rules that hide a review from its adverse party, show an overseer only the reviews a live monitor mandate names, and omit respondent identifiers are SQL predicates and kernel calls inside lib/authority/store/review-intake.ts, so any other query that runs in an organization context can read every review of the organization and the database enforces none of those rules.

POST /api/reviews accepts up to eight adverseUserIds and normaliseAdverse tests each only with isPrincipalId (a non-empty string of at most 255 characters with no control character) plus a self and duplicate check; registerReview then stores them in adverse_user_ids with no lookup showing that the named person is a member of the organization, no trigger checks them (the actor trigger guards opened_by only), and the own-list query excludes a stored adverse id and the kernel decideReview denies oversight to it (ADVERSE_PARTY: respondent cannot exercise oversight), so a complainant decides, by an unverified assertion, which person is excluded from seeing the review and from overseeing it.

POST /api/reviews applies no rate limit of its own, never reads the idempotency key and never uses the ue_authority_requests idempotency store, and the table declares no uniqueness over the opener, type and adverse parties, so every call by an active member inserts a new review, the authority event row the trigger records and a canonical audit row; ue_authority_reviews is append-only (a trigger refuses DELETE and TRUNCATE), so a member or a script can create an unbounded number of permanent review rows that no route or retry path can remove.

POST /api/reviews reads the body with request.json() before openSchema.safeParse, so the schema limits (reviewType enum, eight adverse ids, 255 characters each) apply only after the whole body has been buffered and parsed; the route sets no body-size cap and imports no public-intake or size guard.

The route takes the organization from getOrganizationIdForUser (the selected-organization cookie checked against active membership) and passes it to the store as the explicit organizationId, but calls withRLSContext(async (tx) => ...) with no context map, so outside the canonical-state mode the transaction binds app.current_org_id from the organization on the auth session or user metadata (orgId = authOrgId) instead; withRLSContext documents that only an explicit { organizationId } enforces exactly one organization, and the route never compares its two resolutions, so a disagreement surfaces only as an empty result or as a database error that the route rethrows.

reviewErrorResponse answers only AuthorityStoreError and the case-authorization errors; any other failure (a database or row-level-security error, the Unauthorized error withRLSContext throws, a binding error) is rethrown with `throw error` from a route that has no wrapper, so the caller receives the framework default server error with no structured body, and the route neither logs nor audits the failure.

GET /api/reviews returns, for each review a live monitor mandate allows, complainantUserId and the standard or privileged classification, and listMemberReviewIntake calls the pure kernel decide for review:monitor and writes no record of the read; the decision, the mandate that supplied it and the reviews disclosed are not stored, so an oversight read of complainant identity cannot be reconstructed afterwards.
